title: StateGuard denies every build option: minerals_remaining is a shortfall, not a budget
description:
StateGuard treats minerals_remaining as a spendable budget. It is a SHORTFALL. So on any base that has accumulated minerals toward its current item, the guard denies EVERY option and base.production degrades to the deterministic tier - including, and especially, the correct choice.

MEASURED END TO END on a live game, turn 42, Morgan Solutions (Morganites):

  base_state: current Colony Pod, minerals_accumulated 27, cost 33, mineral_surplus 7
  metrics:    minerals_remaining 6
  action_space (every entry): effects {"minerals_remaining": -<full item cost>}
      unit:0   Colony Pod           cost 33  turns_if_switched 5  turns_if_continued 1
      unit:1   Formers              cost 22  turns_if_switched 4
      unit:2   Scout Patrol         cost 11  turns_if_switched 2
      unit:256 Synthmetal Garrison  cost 22  ...  (and four facilities at 44-220)

  agent chose unit:0 - the item already in production, 27/33 banked, ONE TURN from completion
  guard advisory: "unit:0 spends 33 minerals_remaining but only 6 is available - the state moved since this was offered"
  submit result:  degraded=true, degrade_reason="guard denied every choice (1 stripped); 1 repair attempt(s) also failed"
  adapter row:    tier=llm, applied=llm_degraded, applied_item_name=Colony Pod

THE CATEGORY ERROR, from both ends:
  - metrics.py:134-139 defines minerals_remaining as "Minerals still needed to finish what this base is building", direction "lower is better".
  - thinker neural.cpp:559-562 emits it as (total_cost - minerals_accumulated), clamped at 0. A shortfall.
  - thinker neural.cpp:351 declares every action's effects as {"minerals_remaining": -cost}, the FULL item cost.
  - hank.py StateGuard then reads "spends 33, only 6 available" and denies.

Nothing here is a state race, so the advisory's "the state moved since this was offered" is also wrong and actively misleading - it sends the reader looking for a concurrency bug that does not exist.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY FALSE POSITIVE:
  1. It denies the ENTIRE action space, not one option. Every item costs more than the shortfall by construction, because the shortfall is at most the cheapest thing the base is already building. So the LLM tier cannot land ANY choice on a base mid-build.
  2. It is hardest on the decision the project most wants right: continuing a nearly-finished item. 27 banked minerals and turns_if_continued=1 is the textbook continuity case that na-61c.2's history work and the play skill's "prefer continuity" guidance exist to get right - and the guard vetoes exactly that.
  3. It is invisible in aggregate as a QUALITY problem. The game still gets a legal item (the deterministic fallback picked the same Colony Pod here), so nothing looks broken; the run just quietly stops being an LLM-tier run. The decision record does say degraded=true, so it IS measurable - degrade_rate on base.production should be near 1.0 on any developed game, which is the number to check.

CANDIDATE FIXES, and the choice matters:
  (a) Stop declaring item cost against minerals_remaining. An item's cost is not a withdrawal from a shortfall. For a SWITCH the meaningful effect is that the accumulated minerals are forfeited; for CONTINUING it is that the shortfall falls to zero. Both are expressible, neither is "-cost".
  (b) Teach StateGuard that a "lower is better" shortfall metric is not a resource pool and must not be treated as an affordability budget. This is the more general fix - the same trap waits for any future metric with that direction.
  (c) Declare cost against a metric that IS a pool. There is no per-base mineral pool in the vocabulary today (minerals_accumulated is not in metrics.py), which is why (a) was reached for.

(b) plus (a) is the honest pair: the guard should not infer a budget from a direction, and the adapter should not declare an effect it cannot mean.

ACCEPTANCE: on a base with accumulated minerals, an agent choosing the item already in production is APPLIED (adapter row tier=llm, applied=llm, not llm_degraded), and no advisory claims the state moved. Add a regression test with a world view shaped like the one above - banked 27, cost 33, minerals_remaining 6.

Found while running na-1wu. It is the reason base.production has no tier=llm/applied=llm row yet, while faction.se has four.

Close commit 668a08a already recorded a live before/after on identical state (turn 42, Colony Pod 27/33: llm_degraded -> llm, degraded=false). title: Decision log records tier=llm applied for decisions the game abandoned (llm_timeout_ms=2500)
description:
The orchestrator records tier=llm, degraded=false, "applied to the game" for decisions the game ALREADY ABANDONED. Measured end to end on a live game at turn 39.

WHAT HAPPENED

Ran the agent-brain loop against a real game: NA_BRAIN=agent, orchestrator up, thinker posting to 127.0.0.1:8000. Answered two decisions through /agent/next + /agent/submit. Both returned:

  {"submitted":"unit:0","applied":["unit:0"],"status":"applied to the game","degraded":false}

and the orchestrator's decision log recorded:

  faction.se       t39 Gaians tier=llm degraded=False chosen=['se:none']
  base.production  t39 Hive   tier=llm degraded=False chosen=['unit:0']

The ADAPTER's own log for the same turn says the opposite. Zero rows with tier=llm out of 66; every base.production and faction.se row reads:

  tier=deterministic  applied=native  fallback_reason="orchestrator unreachable or slow"

So the game asked, gave up, applied Thinker's own pick, and moved on. The answer I submitted minutes later was accepted by an orchestrator that had no idea the decision was dead, and written into the record of truth as a successful LLM-tier decision that was applied. It was not applied. Nothing in the decision log distinguishes it from a real one.

ROOT CAUSE, two defects

1. THE TIMEOUT DEFAULT CONTRADICTS ITS OWN DOCUMENTATION.
   thinker src/main.h:180  -> `int llm_timeout_ms = 2500;`
   thinker src/na_http.cpp:285 -> "timeout_ms <= 0 means wait indefinitely, which is the
   configured default."
   Those cannot both be true, and the code wins: the adapter waits 2.5 seconds. thinker.ini
   ships without an llm_timeout_ms line, so 2500 is what every run gets.

   .claude/skills/play-alpha-centauri/SKILL.md tells the agent "The game blocks while you
   think ... there is no clock on your reasoning." That is false against this build by three
   orders of magnitude. An attached agent cannot answer in 2.5s; a human-driven one certainly
   cannot. So on the current default the agent brain CANNOT EVER win the race, and every
   agent-tier run silently degrades to Thinker while reporting success.

2. THE ORCHESTRATOR CANNOT KNOW, AND CLAIMS ANYWAY.
   /agent/submit returns "status":"applied to the game". It has no signal from the adapter that
   the application happened - the adapter already returned native_choice to the engine and hung
   up. A pending decision is never expired, so an answer arriving after the game moved on is
   indistinguishable from one that arrived in time.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A NORMAL BUG

It corrupts the record of truth in the direction that flatters us. docs/observability.md 5.4
exists to catch "a run of pure fallbacks that completes and looks green". This is that failure
inverted and made invisible: the fallbacks ARE recorded, correctly, in the adapter log - and the
orchestrator writes a second, contradictory record marking them llm-tier successes. Every number
derived from the decision log is affected: coverage, degrade_rate, tier attribution, directive
attention and override rates (na-mmp), and any A/B outcome measurement (na-6db). A measurement
that reads 'the LLM tier decided this' when Thinker decided it cannot be corrected after the
fact, because both records look well-formed.

It also invalidates the obvious reading of na-1wu / na-ckn. Submitting successfully and seeing
tier=llm in the decision log is NOT evidence the loop closed. The only proof is a tier=llm row in
the ADAPTER's na-observations.jsonl, or applied_item matching what the agent chose.

FIX

- Short term, unblocks the P0s: set llm_timeout_ms explicitly. 0 for the documented
  wait-indefinitely behaviour, or a large finite value (300000) so an unanswered decision cannot
  freeze the game forever. Either way thinker.ini must carry the line rather than inherit 2500.
- Reconcile main.h:180 with na_http.cpp:285. One of them is lying and the comment is the one
  people read.
- The orchestrator must stop asserting what it cannot observe. Either expire a pending decision
  once the adapter's deadline has passed and record it as abandoned, or have the adapter confirm
  application and only then finalise the record. "status":"applied to the game" should be
  reported by the side that applied it.
- Correct the SKILL's "no clock on your reasoning" line to state the real bound.

Note there is already a related commit, thinker 267275a "fix(neural): record a cached decision
that the board overtook" - same family (an answer arriving after the world moved), different
path.

VERIFY BY MECHANISM, NOT BY THE REPORTING INTERFACE: two logs disagreed here and the one that
was easy to read was the wrong one.
close_reason: All four of the bead's own fix items verified done in code, not by commit message: (1) llm_timeout_ms now provisioned and brain-coupled (87e3147, mine); (2) main.h/na_http.cpp comment reconciled (692080d) — 2500 correctly retained for non-agent brains; (3) orchestrator stops asserting what it cannot observe (bf3170e) — _accepted_status no longer says 'applied to the game', AgentBrain abandons before the engine via ABANDON_MARGIN_SECONDS, late submits get 409 telling the agent not to resubmit; (4) SKILL.md:12 corrected. Full suite 477 passed 0 failed. Residual late-finish path is now REPORTED as late rather than recorded as an applied llm decision — the silent flattering misrecord this bead was about is gone. Dead-process pendings remain na-bzd.

comments.text:
ADAPTER HALF LANDED — NeuralAmplifier 87e3147. Orchestrator half is NOT done (na-bzd).
(ellie, 2026-08-02)

MEASURED WHAT WAS ACTUALLY LEFT, because two of this bead's four fix items were already done:

  [DONE, 692080d] Reconcile main.h:197 with na_http.cpp:285. The comment now states the truth
                  ("that is the INTENDED default and it is NOT what ships").
  [DONE]          SKILL.md "no clock on your reasoning" — line 12 now reads "but only for
                  llm_timeout_ms, and the built-in default is ...".
  [DONE, 87e3147] thinker.ini must carry the line rather than inherit 2500.  <- this commit
  [NOT DONE]      The orchestrator must stop asserting what it cannot observe.  -> na-bzd

THE GAP WAS NARROWER AND WORSE THAN THE BEAD STATES. The bead says "thinker.ini ships without an
llm_timeout_ms line". True, but the repo's thinker.ini has no llm block AT ALL — play-thinker.sh
WRITES one (llm_factions, llm_endpoint) and omitted llm_timeout_ms. So the provisioner that
exists to configure the gate was the thing that left the timeout inherited. Grepped the whole
tree: before this commit llm_timeout_ms appeared only in docs, comments and tests, and in NO
file the engine reads.

AND 2500 IS NOT ITSELF A BUG — worth stating, because "raise the default" is the obvious wrong
fix. main.h chooses it "to cover a Haiku call on a warm connection", which is right for the LLM
tier and is what keeps a dead orchestrator from hanging a turn (invariant 9). It is wrong only
for the ONE brain invariant 9 already carves an exception for. AGENTS.md:59-66 documents that
exception and says to set "NA_AGENT_TIMEOUT (and llm_timeout_ms on the adapter)" — so this was a
documented requirement that nothing implemented.

FIX: the timeout now follows the brain, which is the coupling AGENTS.md requires.
    NA_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS set -> that value      NA_BRAIN=agent -> 300000      else -> 2500
All three verified, plus idempotence against the real play dir (an ini already carrying
llm_timeout_ms=0 is left alone and the value reported, matching the existing llm_factions rule).
Finite rather than 0 deliberately: <=0 means wait indefinitely, and an unattended run that hangs
forever is what NA_TIMEOUT exists to catch (na-ie9) — under Xvfb a hung game looks exactly like
a working one.

The script now WARNS when it takes 2500 with no NA_BRAIN set. The silence was the defect.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX, so nobody reads this as closing the P0: the orchestrator still returns
"status":"applied to the game" for something it cannot observe, and a pending decision from a
dead game is still accepted. Until na-bzd lands, the decision log can still record a tier=llm
success for a decision the game abandoned — this commit only stops the agent from LOSING the
race by construction. Leaving na-t3h OPEN for that reason.

VERIFY BY MECHANISM, per this bead's own closing line: the proof an agent decision landed is a
tier=llm row in the ADAPTER's na-observations.jsonl, or applied_item matching what the agent
chose — never the orchestrator's own record.

title: Play a turn with Claude Code driving via MCP
description:
Supersedes the transport half of na-ckn. Everything is built and verified without a game; this is the run that needs one.

  1. $SMAC_DIR present, 'just game verify' clean.
  2. thinker.ini: llm_factions=2, llm_endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8000, llm_timeout_ms=0 (wait indefinitely).
  3. 'just play' — orchestrator with NA_BRAIN=agent.
  4. claude mcp add neural-amplifier, then let the play-alpha-centauri skill drive.
  5. Confirm: the game blocks at a base.production decision, next_decision returns a world view built from LIVE engine state, submit_orders changes what the base builds.
  6. Then kill the agent mid-decision with NA_AGENT_TIMEOUT set and confirm the game degrades to the deterministic tier instead of hanging.

Watch specifically for the window going 'not responding': the DLL slices its wait and calls PeekMessage(PM_NOREMOVE) without dispatching, deliberately, to avoid re-entering the engine from inside mod_base_build. If the window is unusable rather than merely stale, that trade needs revisiting - do NOT fix it by dispatching messages.
notes:
THE LOOP CLOSES. First adapter-side proof, 2026-08-02, live game:

  {'surface_id':'faction.se','turn':41,'faction':'Gaians','tier':'llm','applied':'llm','fallback_reason':None}

An attached Claude Code agent claimed a decision from a live engine via POST /agent/next, answered it via /agent/submit, and the ENGINE applied it. Verified in na-observations.jsonl (the adapter's own log), not in the orchestrator's - see na-t3h for why the orchestrator's record cannot be trusted for this.

Setup that made it work, all from step 2 of this bead: llm_factions=2 (Gaians, faction_id 1), llm_endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8000, llm_timeout_ms=0. The last of those is load-bearing and the bead was right to name it: the built-in default is 2500ms and NO attached agent can meet it (na-t3h).

STILL OUTSTANDING for this bead:
  - Step 5 names base.production specifically. The surface proven is faction.se. The path is shared (na_decide_* -> na_http_post -> apply) so the mechanism is surface-agnostic, but the literal check has not been made: no tier=llm base.production row exists yet. Driving turns 41->42 produced no Gaians base.production decision, and the turn stopped advancing at 42 (the scripted TURN COMPLETE / confirm clicks stop working there - a unit awaiting orders, most likely).
  - Step 6 (kill the agent mid-decision with NA_AGENT_TIMEOUT set, confirm the game degrades rather than hangs) has NOT been run.
  - Step 4 used the HTTP agent endpoints directly rather than 'claude mcp add'. mcp_server.py wraps the same /agent/next + /agent/submit, so this is a thin difference, but it IS a difference and the bead says MCP.

Two operational traps found while doing it, both of which cost real time:
  - The orchestrator survives game restarts and keeps pendings from DEAD game processes, which then look like live work. Restart the orchestrator whenever you restart the game, and confirm /agent/waiting is empty before trusting the queue.
  - 'orchestrator unreachable or slow' is one message for two different causes (connection refused vs deadline passed). A decision that fired while the port was momentarily free is indistinguishable from one that timed out.

BASE.PRODUCTION REACHED THE LLM TIER (turn 42, Morgan Solutions, Morganites):

  adapter row: tier=llm, applied=llm_degraded, applied_item_name=Colony Pod

So step 5's transport half is proven on base.production, not just faction.se: the game blocked, /agent/next returned a world view built from live engine state (base_state, metrics, an eight-item action space with costs and both turn estimates, run_id, history), and the answer went back through the apply path.

BUT the choice did NOT change what the base builds, and the reason is a new P0: na-co2. StateGuard denied the entire action space because it reads minerals_remaining (a SHORTFALL - minerals still needed, 6 here) as a spendable budget, while every action declares effects of the full item cost (33). Every option therefore looks unaffordable by construction, the decision degraded, and the deterministic tier's pick was applied. `applied=llm_degraded` is the adapter recording that honestly.

title: -na-autoload: exit the main menu after loading (menu-to-session transition)
description:
-na-autoload (thinker fork 2b82af5) successfully loads a savegame - mod_load_daemon returns SAVE_LOAD_VALID (status 0) against a real Autosave_<year>.sav, verified on the gaming host. But the game stays on the main menu, so the loaded state is unreachable.

Clearing *GameHalted is not sufficient. The engine does more of the menu-to-session transition inside load_game (engine.cpp:1057, address 0x5AAAB0) than state loading alone - probably tearing down the menu's own modal loop and entering the main interface. load_game takes (int, int) and addresses saves by slot, which is why it cannot be called directly for an arbitrary path.

Candidate approaches, cheapest first:
1. Identify what load_game does around its call to load_daemon (the call site is hooked at patch.cpp:639, address 0x5AAD7D) and replicate the surrounding steps. Disassembly of 0x5AAAB0..0x5AAD7D would answer it directly.
2. Find the menu's modal loop exit condition and set it alongside GameHalted.
3. Drive the menu with synthetic input instead. xdotool is installed and CAN see the Wine window ('Wine Desktop'), so sending the load-game keystrokes is feasible. Brittle and resolution-dependent, but it needs no engine RE and would unblock unattended runs today.

Approach 3 is the pragmatic unblock; 1 is the correct fix.
acceptance_criteria: Launching with -na-autoload <save> results in a playable in-game session with no human input; na-observations.jsonl shows base.production lines appearing without anyone touching the keyboard
notes:
Starting the QUICK START trace: the label 'QUICK START' does not appear as a string in terranx.exe, in any *.txt in the game directory, or in the 00000409.256 localization resource. So the startup menu is NOT a popp/Script.txt dialog - which rules out the cleanest intervention (intercepting the menu's popp call and answering it programmatically) and means the buttons are drawn from a graphical resource with the dispatch table in code.

Consequence: finding the QUICK START handler needs the menu's click-dispatch code located by structure rather than by string reference. Suggested route: the startup menu is drawn as a Console/Win, and gui.cpp already declares thiscall wrappers for the main-menu class at 0x5FB100 and neighbours (CMAINMENU_ADDSUBMENU_F etc.) - that class is the place to start, since whatever owns the buttons owns their handlers.

Note this does NOT invalidate the strategy in the previous note. Starting a game normally and then swapping state via the replay path is still the right shape; only the means of triggering 'start a game normally' is still open. If QUICK START proves awkward to invoke, any path that establishes a session will do, including a scripted new-game start.
close_reason: SOLVED. -na-autoload reaches a playable session unattended: click QUICK START (opens nothing modal), press Enter to confirm PLANETFALL, then run the engine's own replay/undo load sequence. Verified end to end with no human input - turn 35 from the target save, GameHalted clear, map rendered, no dialog. Key insight: stop constructing the menu-to-session transition and let the engine perform it, then swap state.

title: base.production sends the deterministic tier's answer to the LLM in the decision request
description:
MEASURED in thinker/src/neural.cpp while building na-qu8's eval. Production behaviour, not an eval artifact.

na_decide_base_production (:1339-1341) builds the request body with:

    na_build_base_production(&w, base_id, native_choice, has_gov, call_seq);

and na_build_base_production writes, UNCONDITIONALLY (:899, :905-906):

    ,"native_choice":<int>
    ,"native_choice_name":"<prod_name>"

`w` IS the POST body — the code says so itself at :1352: 'The record and the request body are
the same bytes, and they differ only by the outcome fields appended after the call returns.'

So on every base.production decision the model is told what the native AI would build, and then
asked what to build.

## The asymmetry is the evidence that this is a bug, not a design

base.hurry does the opposite, and does it deliberately. na_decide_base_hurry (:2288) passes
native_hurried = -1, and na_build_base_hurry writes native_choice only `if (native_hurried >= 0)`
(:2235-2236). The DECIDE path withholds the native answer; only the OBSERVE path (which passes 0)
records it. Somebody thought about exactly this hazard on one surface and used a sentinel to
suppress it. base.production has no such parameter.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

It is an ANCHOR on every measurement taken through this surface. na-6db asks whether LLM-tier
decisions produce better outcomes than the deterministic tier; agreement between the tiers is the
headline number there, and agreement with an answer you were shown is not evidence of independent
judgement. The confound points the same way as the hoped-for result, which is the worst direction.

It also silently weakens invariant-1 style reasoning: 'the model picked the legal thing' is less
impressive when the legal thing was named in the prompt.

## Fix, and the care it needs

Give na_build_base_production the same suppression base.hurry has — a sentinel that omits
native_choice/native_choice_name from the REQUEST while keeping them in the OBSERVATION record.
The two must stay distinguishable: the record needs the native answer (it is what 'llm chose X,
applied Y' is measured against); the request must not carry it.

DO NOT fix by stripping the field in the orchestrator. The adapter owns the payload (invariant 2)
and the record and request are built from the same buffer by design — splitting them in the
consumer would put the knowledge in the wrong component and leave the record depending on it.

## Blast radius on committed work

na-htm's 8 committed prompts contain native_choice (2 occurrences each). For its two
base.production decisions that is FAITHFUL to production and must not be silently 'fixed' — the
eval would then measure something we do not ship. For its faction.se / faction.tech decisions the
field may be an observe-only artifact and the prompts would be unfaithful; that needs the same
per-surface check done here. Either way na-uwp (the paid run) should not be spent until this is
settled, because both readings change what the money buys.

The three older evals are CLEAN (0 occurrences) — they use the hand-built harness fixture, which
predates captures.

title: information_value is FLAT on real grounding — it splits the option name on an em dash no retriever emits
description:
Found while re-pinning na-htm after the na-dhs fix. MEASURED, not inferred.

`information_value(fact, label)` is the rule na-373 tested and na-htm exists to re-test. It
scores a fact by the words it adds BEYOND the option's own name. `rank_lines` derives that name
with:

    label_of(line) = line.split(" ", 1)[1].split(" — ")[0]

It splits on an EM DASH. Only na-373's hand-written VERBOSE fixture uses that separator. Every
fact a real retriever emits uses "; " — both `QuipuRetriever.format_row` and
`DatalinksRetriever.describe(compact=True)`.

So on real grounding `label_of` returns the WHOLE fact, `known` becomes every word in it, and
the only "fresh" words left are the id tokens:

    line     unit:colony-pod Colony Pod; founds a new base elsewhere; does not grow ...
    label_of 'Colony Pod; founds a new base elsewhere; does not grow the base th...'
    fresh    ['unit', 'colony-pod']        <- the ID PREFIX, not the content

Measured over all 40 facts pinned for na-htm across its four decisions:

    2 distinct scores in total:  score 2 x36,  score 1 x4

The rule is FLAT. And `rank_lines` sorts stably, so ranking 20 facts that all score 2 returns
them in retriever order unchanged. Confirmed on the artifacts: after the na-dhs re-pin took
base.production t135 from 7 to 20 facts, `.all.task.txt` changed and `.ranked.task.txt` DID NOT
— the ranked arm is still the first four units.

## Why this blocks na-uwp rather than being a tidy-up

The `ranked` arm is therefore not "the 4 most informative facts". It is "the first 4 in
action-space order". Both halves of the eval degrade to measuring action-space POSITION:

  - the choice half compares a truncation against its own prefix;
  - the citation-rank half asks where citations sat in an order that carries no information,
    so it measures whether the model cites early options.

na-htm's dominance gate would NOT catch this. The gate checks that no single fact or decision
owns the citation pool, which would still pass — the pool would be properly spread across four
decisions and be measuring the wrong thing anyway. Caught only by looking at the rule's own
output distribution, which is worth remembering: a guard catches the failure it was built for.

Same class as na-vbe's ("the fixture was never the payload") and na-61c2's ("an eval's arms are
part of the eval"). Third instance, so it is a pattern here, not an accident.

## The fix, and the care it needs

Take the option name as the text before the EARLIEST separator of EITHER kind (" — " or "; ").
That yields the right name for both formats:

    "Recycling Tanks — cost 4; Bonus Resources; needs Biogenetics"  -> "Recycling Tanks"
    "Colony Pod; founds a new base elsewhere; does not grow ..."    -> "Colony Pod"

Splitting on "; " FIRST would be wrong: it gives "Recycling Tanks — cost 4" on the verbose
format and quietly changes na-373's ranking.

CHANGING THIS CHANGES THE RULE UNDER TEST. It alters na-373's `ranked` arm, so its committed
answers stop being evidence about it — acceptable, since na-373 is already withdrawn AND already
stale (na-og3), but it must be recorded rather than absorbed. na-htm has no answers yet, so it
costs nothing there; re-pin and regenerate prompts after.

Verify the fix by DISTRIBUTION, not by the tests passing: re-run the 40-fact scoring above and
require substantially more than two distinct values. A rule that discriminates nothing is the
failure, so the check has to be that it discriminates.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
FIXED and VERIFIED GREEN. Commit f8b5153 on main.

## The hint in my dispatch was wrong, and checking it was worth the two minutes

The dispatch said: "these 8 mypy errors postdate b99b3ba, so check whether
3a0158a/d66ed84/e65c19e introduced them." None of those three touched either file. What actually
happened is simpler: **turns.py did not exist at b99b3ba.** It was ADDED by 2e3fee0
(feat(turns): the turn as a whole, not the oldest decision, na-8ja phase 3), and the errors
arrived with it. My own first query missed this because I filtered on
`src/neural_amplifier/turns.py` and the real path is `orchestrator/src/neural_amplifier/turns.py`
— a path filter that matches nothing returns silence, which reads exactly like "no commits
touched it". Control-test a zero before believing it.

Discriminator run before touching anything, so this was not a guess: checked out b99b3ba in a
detached worktree and ran mypy against it TODAY. Clean, 32 source files. So this is a code
change, not toolchain/dependency drift. Current main checks 35 files — the three new ones are
orders.py, outcomes.py, turns.py.

## Root cause: one, not seven

`_extra()` in turns.py returned `object | None`. Every caller fed that straight into a narrower
field — `DecisionSlot.base_id` is `int | None`, `base` is `str | None`, and the slot key is
`tuple[str, int | None]`. The `object` poisoned the key tuple and then every use of it. Seven
errors, one origin.

**The type checker was reporting a real hole, not being fussy.** Extras come off the wire from an
adapter with no schema at this seam, and pydantic does NOT coerce them, because they are extras
on WorldView rather than declared fields. A `base_id` arriving as "12" would have been stored in
a field declaring it an int — no exception, no warning, just every later read quietly wrong. A
cast to silence mypy would have preserved exactly that hole and destroyed the evidence of it.

Fix: `_extra` now takes the expected type and CHECKS it with isinstance. A present-but-wrong-typed
extra becomes None — the same answer as absent, since neither yields a usable value — and it is
LOGGED, because absent and malformed have completely different causes and a silent coercion
leaves a bad adapter undiagnosable.

The eighth error was independent and trivial: a stale `# type: ignore[arg-type]` at
service.py:565 that suppressed nothing (the isinstance guard three lines above already narrows
`raw_args`), so mypy flagged it as unused.

## Verified by mechanism

    before (main 03eb33e)   mypy: 8 errors in 2 files
    after  (local)          mypy: Success, no issues in 35 source files
    tests                   524 passed, 4 skipped  (was 521 — +3 new)
    ruff check              All checks passed
    ruff format             69 files already formatted
    CI on f8b5153           Orchestrator (Python) SUCCESS  <- the job that was red
                            Pre-commit checks SUCCESS
                            Docs (lint + book) SUCCESS
                            Thinker adapter (MinGW) SUCCESS

Three tests added, including the POSITIVE CONTROL — one asserting a correctly-typed extra still
reads through unchanged. Without it the two wrong-type tests would pass just as well against an
`_extra` that returned None for everything. The tests exist because a future "simplification"
back to a cast would leave mypy green while restoring the hole.

## What this unblocks

This was the top of the lane and it gated everything after it. NeuralAmplifier has never had a
release, and a release cannot be cut over a red main — so the release gap on this repo was this,
not neglect (see aegis-e5vor).

title: Exercise turn-scoped play against a running game — none of na-8ja has met a real turn
description:
na-8ja built all four phases of turn-scoped play and NONE of it has been exercised against a
running game. That is the gap this bead closes.

WHAT IS PROVEN TODAY
  - 521 orchestrator tests, including the negative cases that carry the design (an unobserved
    order is `unknown`, a half-working batch is not `ok`, status never walks backwards)
  - the adapter halves are in the deployed thinker.dll (776bd2ac) and confirmed present by
    strings, not merely in source
  - tests/run-na-tests.sh --with-orchestrator passes 43 checks under Wine against a live service
  - the JSON each emitter produces has been posted to a running orchestrator and read back

WHAT IS NOT PROVEN
  A turn has never been played through any of it. Specifically, no evidence exists that:
    - the adapter's turn announcement fires at mod_turn_upkeep in a real game, or that its
      forecast resembles the decisions that follow
    - an order written to na-command is picked up by a running game and applied
    - is_known refuses a genuinely unexplored tile rather than refusing everything or nothing
    - a batch of >1 line is read as a batch by the real tick (the tests use a fake adapter)
    - an outcome POST reaches the orchestrator from inside a game rather than from curl

THE ONE MOST LIKELY TO BE WRONG, and worth checking first: order/decision mutual exclusion. It
rests on the decision wait not dispatching messages, so na_command_tick cannot run while a
decision is outstanding. That is a property the code has for an unrelated reason, nothing
asserts it, and if it is not true in practice an order could mutate the board from inside a
decision hook — which is the failure mode the wait was written to avoid in the first place.

SHAPE OF THE RUN
  NA_GAME_DIR=<play dir> NA_BRAIN=agent, game resumed from a late save, then:
    1. read GET /turn — does the announcement arrive, and does it name real bases?
    2. issue_order skip on a unit, and confirm from the game that it took
    3. issue_order move onto an explored tile, then onto an unexplored one — expect the second
       refused by name
    4. issue_orders with several lines, and confirm ONE round trip and per-order results
    5. answer a base.production decision, then read /outcome for it
  Each step is a claim the current tests cannot make.

Pairs with na-43h, which also needs a live game and has its own acceptance to run.

the tree under test, NA_BRAIN=agent with a scripted driver answering so no model spend.

## 1. Turn announcement — WORKS

    GET /turn -> turn 135, announced: true, 307 slots
    counts {expected: 237, applied: 67, raised: 1, answered: 2}

na_announce_turn fired at mod_turn_upkeep in a real game and forecast every base of every routed
faction. Arriving decisions MATCHED their forecast slots — the applied 67 are announced entries
that progressed, not duplicates — so the (surface, base_id) key holds against real adapter
records. `unraised` tracked the 237 not yet reached, which is the forecast-vs-reality distinction
doing its job rather than a discrepancy.

## 2. Orders reach a running game — WORKS

    skip 0  -> refused "faction 0 is not routed to the orchestrator (llm_factions)"  waited 0.201s
    skip 6  -> ok "veh 6 ends its turn"

Written to na-command, picked up by the real tick within ONE poll interval, executed, answered.
The first refusal is correct: veh 0 is native life, excluded by llm_enabled's faction_id > 0.

## 3. The turn gate — WORKS, and is informative

    move 7 ...  -> "not faction 3's turn (current is 7)"
    move 8 ...  -> "not faction 5's turn (current is 7)"

Refusals name BOTH factions, which is what made it possible to find a routed unit at all without

title: Turn-scoped agent play: see the whole turn, get execution feedback, and defer a decision to chain dependent moves
description:
Stiwi, 2026-08-02, direct: the playing agent must be able to (1) see ALL events for a turn,
(2) make decisions against that whole picture, (3) receive feedback from execution, and
(4) DELAY a decision until other moves have been made, so it can chain dependent moves across
units and build decisions.

Today it can do none of those four. The agent plays strictly one decision at a time, blind to
its siblings, and never learns what happened. This bead is the design, with the constraint
measured rather than assumed, because one of the four is structurally harder than the other
three and one is nearly free.

## What exists today (read 2026-08-02)

Orchestrator routes (service.py): /health, /decide, /coverage, and — only when the brain is an
AgentBrain — /agent/next, /agent/directive, /agent/submit, /agent/waiting.
`/agent/next` claims THE OLDEST SINGLE pending decision. There is no turn view and no batch.

Adapter (thinker src/neural.cpp): POSTs `/decide` and nothing else — 4 call sites, one per
instrumented surface. **There is no callback of any kind.**

## Constraint 1 — the decision hook is synchronous and must answer NOW

`na_decide_base_production` (neural.cpp:1230-1296) is called by the engine inside the build
hook, POSTs /decide, blocks up to `conf.llm_timeout_ms`, and `return applied;` hands an item id
straight back to the engine, which consumes it immediately. There is no return value meaning
"ask me later". Comment at :1180 says it outright: "Synchronous because the engine is not
thread-safe and mod_base_build's signature ...".

So "defer" cannot mean "return nothing". Any deferral must be a provisional answer that is
later REVISED.

## Constraint 2 — and this is the enabler: for base.production the LAST answer wins

neural.cpp:278-286, and it is measured, not assumed:

    The engine asks the same base for a production choice several times in one turn:
    mod_base_reset is hooked at eleven call sites (patch.cpp:859-869) and each one runs
    mod_base_build followed by mod_base_change — so every call *applies* its own answer,
    and the last one to run is what the base actually builds.

    Measured in real play: 21 of 24 base-turns fired twice, 11 of those pairs
    disagreeing on the choice.

Revision is therefore not a feature to invent — it is already how the engine behaves. An agent
that answers base #1 provisionally, learns what bases #2..#51 need, and revises base #1 on its
second call is using the engine's own semantics.

**This does NOT generalise across surfaces.** `base.hurry` spends energy credits irreversibly at
apply time (it is the one na.toml singles out as "the one that spends something irreversibly").
A provisional "yes, hurry" cannot be taken back. Deferral there can only mean "decline now, and
be willing to be re-offered", which is a different and weaker guarantee.

## Constraint 3 — execution feedback ALREADY EXISTS and is thrown away

This is the cheapest of the four by a wide margin. The adapter already computes the outcome and
writes it to the local `na-observations.jsonl`, and simply never sends it:

  - per decision (neural.cpp:1281-1292): `tier`, `applied`, `applied_item`, `applied_item_name`,
    and `fallback_reason` when it fell back.
  - post-apply verification (`na_verify_base_production`, :1322-1357): reads the base's item back
    AFTER the apply and emits a separate `"event":"divergence"` record when the engine did not
    keep what was decided — explicitly designed to catch "rules we have not learned yet".

So the orchestrator's picture of its own effect is not merely incomplete, it is absent, while the
adapter holds it in full. Routing it back is plumbing, not new observation.

## Recommended build order

**Phase 1 — outcome feedback (small, no blocking-semantics change, do this first).**
Adapter POSTs the outcome fields it already has, keyed by decision id, either as a new
`POST /outcome` or piggybacked on the next `/decide`. Orchestrator stores it against the
decision record and exposes `/agent/outcomes`. Also carries the `divergence` event, which is the
part an agent most needs and can least infer. Satisfies (3) outright.

**Phase 2 — turn-scoped view (medium).**
The orchestrator cannot show a turn it has not been told about: at the moment base #1 is asked,
bases #2..#51 have not been POSTed yet. So the adapter must ANNOUNCE the turn's decision set up
front. `mod_turn_upkeep` is the seam — neural.cpp:2719-2722 describes it as "the engine's
between-turns seam ... hooked into control_turn". Expose `/agent/turn` returning the announced
set plus per-decision status (pending / provisional / answered / applied / diverged).
Satisfies (1) and most of (2).

**Phase 3 — defer and chain (largest, and surface-scoped).**
`/agent/defer` marks a claimed decision provisional: the adapter applies the engine's native
answer for this call and the agent revises on a later call within the same base-turn, relying on
last-answer-wins. Requires:
  - a per-surface `revisable` flag in the frozen registry (surfaces.py). base.production yes;
    base.hurry NO; faction.tech / faction.se need checking, they fire once per faction-turn.
  - the adapter to keep the decision open in its cache and re-raise it (na_cache_put /
    na_history_put already track per-base-turn state).
  - a hard rule that the LAST call of a base-turn cannot be deferred — there is no later call to
    revise in, and a deferral there silently becomes the native answer. This is the failure mode
    to design against: a defer that quietly turns into "the engine decided" reads in the record
    as an agent choice.

## Why phases, and not one change

Phase 1 is pure gain and independent. Phase 3 changes what an answer MEANS, so it should land
after the agent can actually see outcomes — otherwise a revision loop is being flown blind, and
"did my revision take" is exactly the question `na_verify_base_production` was written to answer.

title: Pendings from a dead game process never expire and still accept answers
description:
A game process that dies mid-decision leaves a pending decision that never expires, and the orchestrator will accept an answer for it indefinitely.

Split out of na-t3h, which fixed the other half (the adapter now states its deadline and the orchestrator abandons on it). That bound only helps while the engine is ALIVE to have set one. If the game process goes away - crash, kill, restart - the deadline it declared is never reached by anything, because nothing is counting down on the orchestrator side once the loop is already blocked.

MEASURED, 2026-08-02. Killed the game, relaunched it, and queried the still-running orchestrator:

  /agent/waiting -> four decisions at turn 40, status "pending", ages 600-1275s

Every one raised by a process that had been dead for twenty minutes. Claiming and answering one returned the usual success response, degraded:false. There was no game to apply it to. They are indistinguishable from live work in the queue, in /agent/waiting, and to an agent polling /agent/next.

Cost when it bites: an agent (or a person) spends real reasoning on a decision that cannot land, and the resulting record is written as a normal decision. It also makes the queue untrustworthy as a signal - "is the game waiting on me?" cannot be answered from it.

SUGGESTED FIX: process identity. The orchestrator already mints a game_id, but per ORCHESTRATOR instance, not per game - which is exactly backwards for this. Have the adapter send a per-run id with every /decide (it can generate one at DLL load), and drop or mark pendings whose run id is not the current one as soon as a new run id is seen. That is cheap and needs no liveness probing.

Weaker alternatives, for the record: an absolute age cap on pendings (crude - a legitimately slow agent looks identical to a dead game), or client-disconnect detection (hard in the sync FastAPI handlers this uses, and the adapter's socket close is not reliably observable there).

ACCEPTANCE: kill a game mid-decision, start a new one, and confirm /agent/waiting does not offer the dead run's decisions - and that submitting to one is refused rather than recorded.

OPERATIONAL NOTE until this is fixed: restart the orchestrator whenever you restart the game, and confirm /agent/waiting is empty before trusting the queue. This cost real time during the na-1wu run: stale pendings looked like live work twice.

title: WorldView.history is never populated - the adapter emits recent_builds instead
description:
The Thinker adapter emits `recent_builds`; the contract field is `history`. Nothing maps one to the other, so `WorldView.history` is None on every real base.production decision and the system prompt's history paragraph describes a field that is never present.

Measured on origin/main (thinker 48e7807, NA fe66430):

  - thinker src/neural.cpp:568 writes `,"recent_builds":[` into the world view; the string `"history"` is never emitted by the adapter.
  - orchestrator/src/neural_amplifier/contract.py:249 declares `history: list[PriorChoice] | None`.
  - `grep -rn recent_builds orchestrator/src/ scripts/` returns NOTHING. No bridge, no alias, no service-side mapping.
  - brain.py:207 tells the model: "If the world view carries a `history` list, those are the choices made for this same subject on recent turns, OLDEST FIRST".
  - thinker neural.cpp:564 `na_write_history` emits NEWEST FIRST, by design ("a brain reading top-down should meet the most relevant entry first").

Three consequences, worst last:

1. The history paragraph in the system prompt is dead text for Thinker play - it gates on a field that is always absent. That is prompt budget spent on nothing.

2. The strong continuity guidance ("treat an unfinished item you chose before as the standing answer") hangs off that same absent field, so the behaviour the 3-arm experiment measured is not the behaviour real play gets.

3. ORDER IS INVERTED. The payload still reaches the prompt, because WorldView is extra=allow and the whole object is dumped - so the model sees `recent_builds` unexplained while holding a documented mental model that says oldest-first. A model that applies the documented reading to the undocumented field reads the OLDEST entry as the most recent choice. That is the na-eaa failure class exactly: a model misreading state it was handed correctly.

The docs already claim this works. docs/decision-inputs.md section 2 lists category 5 as `history` and carries a three-arm result (0.30 / 1.00 / 0.10) showing history drives continuity without anchoring. That experiment set `history` directly on a synthetic world view; no adapter output can currently populate it, so the measured benefit does not transfer to a real game. Nothing is wrong with the experiment - the wire is missing under it.

Fix is small; pick one and say which:
  - adapter-side: emit `history` in PriorChoice shape (turn/item/tier), oldest first, and retire `recent_builds`; or
  - orchestrator-side: map `recent_builds` -> `history` where the world view is parsed, reversing order.

Adapter-side is preferable - the contract is what both engines must speak, and GLSMAC will need the same field. Whichever is chosen, ORDER MUST BE RECONCILED, and test_history_survives_as_an_engine_dependent_passthrough (orchestrator/tests/test_adapter_contract.py:369) needs revisiting: it asserts recent_builds is deliberately NOT a contract field, which is the decision that has since been contradicted by adding one.

Acceptance: a base.production world view captured from a live game parses with `world_view.history` non-empty, entries oldest first, and `tier` populated; the fixture in test_adapter_contract.py matches what the adapter actually emits.

Found while verifying na-61c.2's real-play acceptance criterion, which is the other half of this: that criterion ("verified across at least 10 consecutive turns of real play showing no oscillation") has no recorded evidence anywhere in the repo - the 3-arm result is same-input sampling, not consecutive turns. Worth its own bead if this one does not cover it.

Verified against live play turns 36-38, not a fixture: WorldView.history parses non-empty, oldest first, every entry strictly in the past, tier and item contract-valid. scripts/check_live_world_view.py reports history PRESENT where it was ABSENT before. All entries read 'deterministic' - nothing was listening on :8000, so the llm-tier path is unexercised in that capture.

title: Close the loop on faction.tech, faction.se and base.hurry
description:
Three of the four instrumented surfaces are observation only: the record is written and the engine's own choice still executes, so the brain watches and has no influence. Coverage counted as applied is 1 of 77, not 4.

Each needs the same thing base.production already has: an apply command that sets the choice, validated against the engine's own availability test so an illegal order is rejected rather than applied, and a decision record at tier=llm on the apply path.

faction.tech - set Factions[f].tech_research_id. Check what the engine does with a mid-research switch, since forfeiting accumulated labs is the same trap as switching a partly built item.
faction.se - the SE choice is applied through social_set / the pending values; needs the cost check the observer already reports, and only fires for AI-slot factions (mod_social_ai returns early for humans).
base.hurry - spends credits, so this is the first apply path that can lose something irreversibly. It needs the affordability check the observer already does, and the snapshot semantics matter: the hook runs after mod_base_hurry.

Turning each on is then a one-line change in surfaces.toml, and the toggle is how it gets rolled out: instrument, watch it observe, then let it decide.

All three apply paths land in scbrown/thinker src/neural.cpp: apply-tech <faction_id> tech:<n>, apply-se <faction_id> se:<field>:<model>|se:none, apply-hurry <base_id> hurry:now|hurry:none. Each validates with the engine's own test rather than a reconstruction — tech_avail, society_avail, and can_hurry_item plus an affordable hurry_cost — so an illegal order is rejected rather than applied, which is the same guarantee the existing apply makes.

Worth recording: faction.se takes legality from society_avail and deliberately does NOT reuse the prerequisite and opposition checks the observation's action space makes for itself. The two are supposed to agree and this is the one that binds. Also both spending paths debit through the engine's own routine (hurry_item does the credit debit and the mineral credit together; social_upheaval prices the change and faction.cpp's sequence charges it) because reimplementing either half is how a faction gets free production.

title: Agent-as-brain: orchestrator serves decisions over MCP
description:
Inversion of control. The orchestrator stops calling a model and starts serving a decision surface; Claude Code (or any MCP client) attaches and answers.

Landed: pending.py (decision queue), agent_brain.py (AgentBrain blocks until answered), doorbell.py (optional tmux nudge), mcp_server.py (next_decision / submit_orders / decisions_waiting), /agent/* endpoints mounted only under NA_BRAIN=agent, and the play-alpha-centauri skill.

Key property: an agent is NOT a privileged client. Its orders go through validate() and the guard and produce the same decision record, because AgentBrain sits exactly where ClaudeBrain sits. 12 of 13 orchestrator modules were already invariant enforcement rather than LLM plumbing, which is why this was one class rather than a second pipeline.

Verified with a real MCP client against a real service: illegal id refused with the legal set, valid id applied, blocked POST /decide returned it, record written tier=llm degraded=false.

title: just check fails on a clean checkout
description:
Found 2026-07-31 while landing A1: 'just check' - the gate AGENTS.md requires before every push - failed on HEAD with no local changes.

Two causes, both fixed in the same change:
  1. The pre-commit ruff-format hook runs from the repo root. Ruff resolves config by walking up from each file, so orchestrator/*.py found orchestrator/pyproject.toml (line-length 100) and scripts/*.py found nothing and fell back to the built-in 88. The hook reformatted the scripts on every run while they were committed at 100. Fixed with a root ruff.toml pinned to the same 100.
  2. docs/directives.md had two fenced blocks with no language (MD040).

Worth recording rather than just fixing: a gate that is always red is one everybody learns to push past, and it had been red long enough that nobody noticed it going redder. 'just check' is now green and idempotent - two consecutive runs both exit 0.

title: Long-horizon directives: measurable strategy that steers tactical decisions
description:
A long-horizon decision (tech, SE, agenda) can reason about a path over many turns, but today its conclusion dies with the response - base.production and base.hurry next turn know nothing about it. Give the LLM's response a way to issue DIRECTIVES that persist and steer later decisions.

The whole design turns on one constraint: a directive may only reference a metric the world view actually reports. That makes it falsifiable instead of vibes - 'keep reserves above 100' can be checked, 'play aggressively' cannot. A directive naming an unreported metric reads as UNMEASURABLE, never as satisfied, because a missing measurement that looks like a passing one is the failure mode that makes the whole mechanism dishonest.

Composes with the doctrine plane (docs/strategy-knowledge.md): doctrine is a curated prior retrieved as grounding, directives are this game's own standing intent.
design: Directives are issued on Orders (the model's response) and injected on WorldView with their live measured value, exactly as grounding is injected. Metrics arrive as an engine-neutral WorldView.metrics dict from the adapter, so the orchestrator never learns where an engine files its economy (invariant 2); metrics.py holds only the vocabulary. increase/decrease comparators capture a baseline at issue time, or they are unmeasurable later.
acceptance_criteria: A directive issued by a faction-level decision is visible, with its current value and satisfied state, in a later base-scope decision record; an unknown or unreported metric is rejected or reported unmeasurable rather than passing.
close_reason: Core mechanism shipped and measured: measurable directives with priorities, value trade-offs, multi-hop entity retrieval and full record instrumentation. base.hurry 0.60 -> 1.00 with 9/10 runs naming the directive. Remaining work split into na-b4v, na-43h, na-mmp.

title: base.hurry is genuinely contested: 0.60 stability at n=10 even fully grounded
description:
base.hurry splits 6/4 between hurry:now and hurry:none over 10 identical prompts on the turn-35 University Base observation (Colony Pod, 5/30 minerals, 81 credits to save 7 turns, 82 in reserve). Utilisation is 0.90, so the brain IS reading the grounding - it just does not resolve the question.

An n=5 run reported 1.00 for the same surface. That was sampling noise, and it is a caution about every 1.00 in the harness: five runs cannot distinguish stable from lucky. Consider raising the harness default.

The hypothesis worth testing is that the missing input is opportunity cost, not rules. 81 of 82 credits is 99% of the treasury, and nothing in the world view says what else that energy could buy or what the faction's income is - base_state carries mineral_surplus but no energy income. A decision about whether a purchase is worth it cannot be made from the price alone.
design: Do NOT chase this with prompt engineering. If the input is genuinely insufficient the fix is a world-view field (energy income, reserve trend, competing sinks); if it is sufficient then 0.60 is the model's honest uncertainty on a close call and the right answer is to measure outcomes (na-6db) rather than consistency.
acceptance_criteria: Either stability rises materially after adding the missing economic inputs, or the surface is documented as a genuine judgement call and routed on outcome evidence instead.
close_reason: Hypothesis confirmed. The surface was short of opportunity cost, not rules: with one priority-7 directive to bank energy credits, base.hurry went from a 6/4 split to unanimous hurry:none over 10 runs, with 9/10 naming the directive as what decided it. Grounding utilisation was already 0.90 before the change, so it was never a retrieval gap. Shipped as the directive mechanism (docs/directives.md); live re-measurement with faction_state tracked in na-b4v.

title: ClaudeBrain sent effort unconditionally, degrading every decision on Haiku 4.5
description:
ClaudeBrain passed output_config={'effort': ...} on every request. Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 reject the effort parameter with a 400, so invariant 9 (degrade safely) returned the native fallback for every decision. This is a self-hiding outage: the stability harness read five identical fallbacks as 'stability 1.00' and the run looked like a well-behaved model.

Fix: gate effort on a cached models.retrieve capability probe, reading the PER-LEVEL flag rather than the coarse effort.supported - Opus 4.5 reports supported:true and still rejects 'max'. A probe that cannot answer omits effort, because losing effort costs decision quality while raising would cost the decision.
design: Queried, not a hardcoded model list: such a list is wrong the moment a model ships. Cached per instance since the answer cannot change for a fixed model id - base.production fires per base per turn, so an uncached probe would double the round trips per decision.
acceptance_criteria: An unsupported (model, level) pair never reaches messages.parse; a real Haiku 4.5 run through the stability harness reports zero degraded runs.
close_reason: Closed

title: Expand the deterministic tier onto the 21 surfaces with no native AI path
description:
21 of the 77 surfaces (surfaces.NO_AI_PATH) are decisions the native AI NEVER makes - base.abandon, base.disband, base.retool, base.governor_config, base.hq_escape, council.vote, council.buy_vote, diplo.base_swap and the rest.

These must NOT get an LLM tier first. Invariant 9 is degrade safely: a slow, broken or over-budget model returns the safe fallback and the game never stalls waiting on the brain. On these surfaces there IS no fallback - no native choice to revert to - so a model failure stalls or corrupts a turn instead of quietly reverting to a competent default. Putting the brain there first inverts the dependency.

So: build the deterministic tier for them FIRST, in the Thinker fork, as an ordinary mod feature - the same way Thinker already improves production and movement AI. Then add the LLM tier on top, following the established pattern (instrument -> ground -> close the loop -> A/B).

Two reasons this ordering is better than a shortcut:
1. The work is independently useful. A better deterministic tier improves the game whether or not a brain is ever attached, which is also how it gets reviewed and trusted upstream.
2. It gives the LLM something to be measured AGAINST. Without a native answer there is no baseline, so 'the brain decided X' cannot be scored - see na-6db, which needs exactly this baseline to A/B against.

Suggested order within the epic, cheapest and most self-contained first: base.retool and base.governor_config (pure base-local rules), then base.abandon / base.disband (need a value judgement about a base but no diplomacy), then the council and diplomacy surfaces (need cross-faction state and are the least self-contained).

Each child should land as a normal Thinker feature with its own config option defaulting to off, so a stock build is unchanged.
design: Do not batch these. Each surface is a separate engine behaviour with its own correctness question, and a broad change to eleven decision paths at once is unreviewable and unbisectable. One surface, one config flag, one probe, one coverage-table row.
acceptance_criteria: For each surface taken on: a deterministic decision function in the fork, gated by a thinker.ini option defaulting to off; the surface then instrumented with a side-effect-free probe; docs/game-surface.md coverage table updated; and the native answer available as the LLM tier's fallback before any LLM routing is enabled
notes:
Blocks na-6db (outcome measurement): without a deterministic baseline on these surfaces there is nothing to A/B the brain against.

Registry list for reference (surfaces.NO_AI_PATH, 21):
  base.abandon, base.disband, base.governor_config, base.hq_escape, base.retool,
  council.buy_vote, council.vote, diplo.base_swap
  ...and 13 more - query with: python -c "from neural_amplifier import surfaces as S; print(sorted(S.NO_AI_PATH))"

title: Enrich the base.production action space with cost and effect
description:
The action space must carry mineral cost, turns at current surplus, category (unit/facility/project) and a one-line effect for every offered item - not just a display name.

A bare name list is not a decidable comparison. 'Formers' vs 'Scout Patrol' cannot be weighed without cost, and a brain that cannot compare cost will systematically over-pick expensive items. This is the single highest-leverage input for decision quality on this surface (docs/decision-inputs.md section 1.1).

contract.Action is extra=allow, so the extra fields are additive and need no schema change. Ship cost and accumulated minerals separately and let the brain divide - do not pre-compute 'turns remaining' for a partially built item, which is where the arithmetic goes subtly wrong.
acceptance_criteria: Every Action in a base.production world view carries id, name, mineral cost, category and effect; the values are read from the engine, not hardcoded; a world view captured from real play is checked against the engine's own numbers
notes:
VERIFIED against a live game, and it was wrong twice. Fixed in thinker fork.

  - Availability: can_build_unit/can_build are NOT availability tests - they never check tech. 125 options for a turn-35 base, including Alien Artifact. mod_veh_avail / mod_facility_avail are the engine's own tests; same base then offers 8, matching the game's build menu.
  - Cost units: engine cost is in 'rows'; minerals = cost * mod_cost_factor, which varies by faction and difficulty. Base state reports minerals_accumulated in raw minerals, so the world view mixed two units - Colony Pod 'cost 3' against 'accumulated 4' reads as nearly affordable and is actually 33 vs 4. Now normalised and labelled cost_unit=minerals.

Verified output for Gaia's Landing, turn 35: 8 actions - Colony Pod 33, Formers 22, Scout Patrol 11, Synthmetal Garrison 33, Recycling Tanks 44, Recreation Commons 44, Human Genome Project 220, Weather Paradigm 220. Facility effect strings populated from alphax.txt via CFacility.effect.

title: Add recent build history to the base.production world view
description:
Record what each base built over the last few turns and include it in the world view.

Production decisions are re-evaluated every turn (several times per turn at the engine level). A stateless brain will flip between two reasonable options turn after turn and accumulate nothing - each individual choice defensible, the sequence useless. Recent history is what makes a stable choice possible, and it is cheap: a short ring buffer per base.

Also record whether the current item was chosen by Claude or by the deterministic tier, so the brain can tell its own past reasoning from Thinker's.
acceptance_criteria: World view carries the last N items built or queued for this base, and the tier that chose the current one; verified across at least 10 consecutive turns of real play showing no oscillation between two options
notes:
Instability now measured properly: 5 byte-identical prompts, 4 chose Colony Pod, 1 chose Formers - stability 0.80 (see na-eaa).

This REVISES the earlier note on this issue. I recorded two runs disagreeing and flagged it as suggestive because the prompts differed; the controlled run shows the disagreement was most likely this same 1-in-5 variance rather than the prompt difference. So the effect is real but smaller than implied.

Does recent build history still matter? Probably yes, but the argument is now weaker and should be tested rather than assumed. A 20% flip rate on a decision re-evaluated every turn still means a base changes its mind roughly every five turns, which accumulates nothing - but that is an inference, and na-eaa's harness plus 10 consecutive turns of real play would settle it. Keep at P1 but verify before building.

title: mod_base_build fires twice per base per turn - decide which call is authoritative
description:
Measured in real play on 2026-07-29 (26 observations, turns 2-5, six factions): every (turn, base_id) pair appears EXACTLY TWICE in na-observations.jsonl, and the two calls return different choices. Gaia's Landing on turn 2 produced both 'Scout Patrol' and 'Formers'.

Cause: mod_base_reset is hooked at eleven engine call sites (thinker src/patch.cpp:859-869) - bases_reset, base_production x5, and four BaseWin entry points - and each calls mod_base_build (src/base.cpp:998).

Why this blocks A1 rather than being cosmetic: orchestrator.py owns 'exactly one decision record per decision, on every path'. If the adapter POSTs on every mod_base_build call, one base-turn produces two LLM decisions - double-counted coverage, double-billed tokens, and two contradictory orders for the same slot. The engine is authoritative about what it asks; we have to decide what constitutes one decision.

Thinker fork commit bd1a6ea now records has_gov (mod_base_build's own second parameter) on each observation so the two calls are distinguishable. Next step is to collect a longer sample and determine whether has_gov alone separates them, or whether the call site must also be identified (which would mean passing a discriminator from each patch site).
design: Candidate rules, cheapest first: (1) has_gov distinguishes them cleanly - filter on it; (2) last-call-wins per (turn, base_id), since the final call is what mod_base_change actually applies; (3) identify the call site by passing a constant from each of the eleven patch sites. Prefer (1) or (2) - (3) touches eleven hook sites and couples the adapter to engine layout.
acceptance_criteria: A rule is documented for which mod_base_build invocation is the decision of record; the adapter emits one observation per decision per base-turn, or emits all of them with a field that unambiguously marks the authoritative one; validated against a sample of at least 20 turns
notes:
VERIFIED in real play 2026-07-29, and the original framing was wrong in an important way.

Sample: 50 base.production records, turns 26-34, 38 distinct (turn, base_id) groups.

  call_seq values seen:      1 x38, 2 x10, 3 x2
  calls per (turn,base):     once x28, twice x8, three times x2
  call_seq unique in group:  38 of 38, zero collisions
  records with call_seq==1:  38 - exactly one per distinct base-turn

So gating on call_seq == 1 provably yields exactly one decision per base-turn. A1's
one-paid-call guarantee holds, and the invariant 'exactly one decision record per
decision' is satisfiable.

CORRECTION to the earlier finding. The title says 'fires twice per base per turn'.
It does not - it fires ONE to THREE times, and most often only once (28 of 38 groups).
The first sample happened to catch a turn where duplication was universal, which made
a variable phenomenon look constant.

This matters concretely: any rule of the form 'take the second call' or 'take the last
call' would have MISSED 28 of 38 decisions entirely, because for those groups there is
no second call. call_seq == 1 is correct precisely because it is the only invocation
guaranteed to exist for every base-turn. Had we settled on last-call-wins - which was

    Some of our units have not yet moved this turn. Do you really want to end the turn now?

unit of the current faction with movement left (engine's own moves_spent vs veh_speed). By
the time we ask to end the turn there are no unmoved units. That is 3.0.2's rule applied -
never open a modal - not an exception to it. Skipping units IS a gameplay decision and is

READ BEFORE QUOTING ANY NUMBER THIS PRODUCES:

  - A two-option surface has a stability FLOOR of 0.50. A coin flip reports 0.50, not 0. The
    original '0.60, the least stable surface we have' is barely distinguishable from random, and
    at n=20 the Wilson interval is roughly +/-0.21 — wide enough that a 0.60 -> 0.75 move is not
    a result. score prints the floor and the intervals so this cannot be read off a point estimate.
  - Stability is NOT the outcome. Hurrying spends 19 of 171 credits irreversibly. score reports
    agreement with the deterministic tier beside stability and names MORE STABLE AND LESS ALIGNED
    as the bad case. If the run lands there, the answer is not 'grounding helped'.
  - If the subject arm cites the offered fact 0 times, there is no treatment and the arms differ
    by run-to-run variance on a near-coin-flip surface. score prints a TREATMENT WARNING for
    exactly this; do not read a difference through it.

treatment is verified (the subject grounds to one fact, both action labels ground to nothing),
and n=20 per arm is the bead's own design. But go in expecting the interval to be wide.

title: harvest-world-views.py cannot see the adapter log — a surface that reaches na-observations.jsonl and not the store is invisible
description:
Found recovering the base.hurry capture (na-qu8, commit fe88784).

There are TWO sinks a world view can land in, and the harvest script reads one:

    NA_WORLD_VIEW_STORE/<hash>.json      <- scripts/harvest-world-views.py reads THIS
    $PLAY_DIR/na-observations.jsonl      <- the adapter's own log, read by NOTHING

na-ibh built the harvest specifically so a rare surface could not be dropped by being
forgotten at the end of a long session. It works, and it has a blind spot: base.hurry sat in
the play directory's na-observations.jsonl from 2026-08-02, and TWO separate sweeps concluded
'no base.hurry capture survives anywhere on disk' — because both searched the repo and /tmp,
and the adapter log lives in the SMAC install, which is neither.

That is the exact failure na-ibh exists to prevent, arriving through the door it does not watch.
Worse than an ordinary gap: the script's existence is what makes people stop looking, so the
uncovered sink is less likely to be searched by hand than before the script existed.

Fix: teach harvest-world-views.py to read $PLAY_DIR/na-observations.jsonl as a second source —
each line is already a full contract world view (the adapter emits the contract directly), so it
needs parsing and newest-per-surface selection, not translation. It should report which sink
each capture came from, so 'the store had it' and 'only the log had it' stay distinguishable.

Verify by mechanism, not by the script exiting 0: delete a surface from the store, leave it in
the log, and require the harvest to still find it. A harvest that cannot demonstrate finding a
log-only surface has not been fixed.

POWER, and read this before spending: the same pre-check measured a ~1-in-3 per-run citation
rate (2 of 3 runs cited nothing at all). 80 calls therefore yields on the order of 25-30 POOLED
CITATIONS, not 80. `score` reports the Wilson interval and prints the n that would separate the
observed gap from chance, so an underpowered result announces itself rather than being quoted —
but going in expecting "cannot distinguish at this n" is the honest prior.

BLOCKED ON na-dhs, and this is the part that would waste the money. QuipuRetriever truncates to
12 LABELS BEFORE querying, so na-htm's base_production_turn135 decision grounds 7 of its 48
options. If na-dhs changes that, the pinned grounding changes, and answers measured against the
old pin are not evidence about the new one. `just eval harvest na-htm` will say so — it prints
the drift and refuses to apply it, precisely because re-pinning means re-answering.

So the order is: settle na-dhs first, re-harvest if it moved, THEN spend.

Recommendation: spend it once na-dhs is settled. The $7 now buys a measurement rather than a
debugging session — arms, pin, scorer and four end-to-end controls all run today for free, and
the scorer has been shown to recover four answers known in advance.

The answers are outdated, not wrong.

**I re-ran NOTHING against a model. Zero of the three.** No arm was re-answered; no tokens were
spent. Every manifest record carries `re_run: false` so a future reader cannot assume otherwise.

What I DID measure (free, re-derivable):

  - the exact prompt diff, per cell
  - that the diff is byte-identical across arms within each eval
  - that `turns_to_completion` appears in no arm's world-view payload and in none of the
    committed prompts
  - which retriever each eval uses, and whether its limit bites

What I REASONED from those measurements: that an addition which is identical on both sides of a
between-arm comparison cannot move that comparison. That is the load-bearing step and it is
reasoning, not measurement. It could be wrong if the added text interacted with the arms
asymmetrically — which is why the record pins the hashes rather than erasing them.

It was the right thing to ask and it is testable for free. All three older evals use
`DatalinksRetriever`, not `QuipuRetriever`. na-dhs was a QuipuRetriever-only defect:

    limit              12
    options in fixture 8
    facts retrieved    8
    limit bites?       False        <- so no truncation, before or after
    has a query step?  False        <- the na-dhs defect was in the SPARQL candidate list

Three independent reasons it cannot compound: wrong class; DatalinksRetriever applies its limit
to RESULTS (append-then-break), never to candidates, so the bug's shape cannot exist there; and
with 8 options against a limit of 12 it never fires anyway.

So "stale" does not understate it by that route. The answers are outdated, not wrong.

    + one metric-VOCABULARY line for `turns_to_completion`
    + "decision_deadline_ms": null
    + "run_id": null

COMMON-MODE: 1 distinct diff per eval across 2, 3 and 2 arms. INERT: `turns_to_completion`
describes a metric these fixtures do not carry — 0 occurrences in every committed prompt and in
every regenerated payload.

I proposed three options on this bead. (a) re-answer, (b) re-hash, (c) mark and leave it red.
I did none of them, because there is a better one and (b) vs (c) is a false choice.

`drift_reviewed` in the manifest stores BOTH hashes — the one the answers were measured against
and the one adjudicated. `prompt_sha256` is never overwritten. So:

  - `check` prints `ok (drift reviewed 2026-08-03 by sattler) — <reason>` for exactly that pair;
  - ANY further change makes a third hash, matches no review, and goes STALE again — naming the
    review that failed to cover it, so a stale adjudication cannot be read as a current one.

precisely when the drift looks harmless. Why not (c): a check that stays red forever gets
ignored — which is how these seven cells went unnoticed in the first place. A pinned
adjudication is the only version that can go green AND go red again.

    red:   perturb _SYSTEM after the review, re-check       -> 7/7 STALE, one line each,

drift. And na-5to still stands: `information_value` is flat on real grounding, which is a defect
in the RULE, not in the prompt these answers were measured against.

title: QuipuRetriever truncates to 12 LABELS before querying, so a 48-option decision grounds 7 options
description:
Found while building na-htm's multi-decision eval (commit d671e1a).

quipu.py retrieve(): `labels = list(dict.fromkeys(candidates))[: self.limit]` — the limit is
applied to the CANDIDATE LABELS before the SPARQL query, not to the facts that come back.

MEASURED, not inferred, against the committed capture base_production_turn135.json
(University, turn 135, 48 build options) with quipu-server on .quipu/na.db:

    48 options in the action space
    12 labels queried (the first 12 in action-space order)
     7 facts returned

So 41 of 48 options reach the model with no grounding at all, and WHICH 41 is decided by
action-space order rather than by anything about the decision.

Why this matters beyond the count: na-373's stated mechanism for how truncation hurts is that
grounding is roughly one fact per option, so dropping a fact removes the argument for a
PARTICULAR option, and an unexplained option loses. If that mechanism is real, it is already
operating on 41 of 48 options before any eval arm acts — silently, and invisibly in the record,
which shows which facts were offered but never which options were left unargued.

Two candidate fixes, and they are not equivalent:
  (a) apply the limit to RESULTS rather than to candidate labels — every option gets asked
      about, and the cut falls on what the store actually knows;
  (b) raise the limit for large action spaces, which trades prompt budget for coverage.

(a) is the one that changes which options are represented; (b) only changes how many. Neither
is obviously right and this needs the budget discipline in docs/quipu-integration.md read
alongside it — filing rather than fixing.

Does not invalidate na-htm: citations there are scored against the ranking of what was
actually offered.

to issue rather than what a directive is". Done. There are TWO directive field descriptions, and
**the model is shown the wrong one.**

### The model-facing schema says nine words, and they are a SUPPRESSOR

`response.py` states its own purpose in its first line:

    "The shapes we ask a model to fill in, as distinct from the shape we pass around."

It exists because the wire contract is `extra="allow"` (unbounded grammar) and too large for
structured output. `brain.py` is its only importer — this IS the structured-output path.

    response.py:113   directives: list[DirectiveOut] = Field(
                          description="Standing intent for FUTURE decisions. Empty unless setting direction."

That is the entire instruction the model receives. It contains NO "when". Its one actionable
clause — "Empty unless setting direction" — points at empty.

### All of the WHEN guidance lives in the schema the model never sees

    contract.py:450   description=(
        "Standing strategic intent to place on FUTURE decisions, WHEN THIS DECISION COMMITS TO A
         PLAN THAT LATER TURNS MUST FOLLOW TO BE WORTH ANYTHING. Leave empty unless you are
         genuinely setting direction. `metric` must be one of the metric names listed in the system
         prompt — a directive naming anything else is discarded, because it could never be checked.
         Use at_least/at_most with a `target` for an absolute bound, or increase/decrease/hold to be
         measured against the value at issue time. Set `horizon_turn` to ..."

~700 characters, including the only sentence that answers "when", the metric constraint, the
bound semantics, and horizon_turn. `contract.py` is the wire contract — "the shape we pass
around". The model never reads it.

The bead cites it: `cited` was explained in the system prompt, came back empty every run, and only
worked once the explanation moved into the schema the model reads. `directives` was given a field
description for that same reason — but it was added to the WRONG SCHEMA. The fix that worked for
`cited` was applied here in form and missed in substance.

So the twenty-run zero is not surprising and does not need a larger sample to confirm. A model
reading "Empty unless setting direction", with no statement of when a directive pays off and no
in-turn payoff, will return empty essentially every time. The measurement was correct; the arm
was never actually installed.

Move the WHEN clause — and only that — into `response.py`'s directives description. Specifically
the "when this decision commits to a plan that later turns must follow to be worth anything" half,
which is the trigger condition, NOT the metric/bound/horizon mechanics (those are validation
concerns and belong where they are).

paste of the 700-char version. Suggested shape, ~25 words instead of 9:

    "Standing intent for FUTURE decisions. Issue one when THIS choice commits to a plan later
     turns must follow to be worth anything; otherwise leave empty."
