title: Faction aggregates read 0 on base.production for factions whose turn is not being processed — a false zero in the setback denominator
description:
Found while running the na-s4e build A/B (evals/runs/na-s4e). NOT caused by that fix — both
build arms agree, so it predates thinker 0722b7b.

On the base.production surface, factions whose turn is not being processed report faction-scope
aggregates as ZERO while other fields on the same record are populated:

    fid=2 Hive        base.production  energy_income 0  labs_output 0   energy_reserves 707  base_count 49
    fid=3 University  base.production  energy_income 0  labs_output 0   energy_reserves 547  base_count 55

A 49-base faction does not have zero gross energy and zero labs output. The same factions report
sane values on other surfaces at the same turn:

    fid=2 Hive        faction.tech     energy_income  6  labs_output  25
    fid=3 University  faction.tech     energy_income 127 labs_output 396
    fid=3 University  faction.se       energy_income 353 labs_output 610

So the aggregates (Faction.energy_surplus_total, turn_commerce_income, facility_maint_total,
labs_total) are evidently not refreshed at the base.production observation point for a faction
whose turn is not currently being processed — while energy_credits and base_count, which are not
per-turn recomputed aggregates, stay correct.

WHY THIS MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A CURIOSITY. metrics.energy_income is the denominator of
setback_turns (directives.py RATE_OF -> _setback). A directive evaluated against one of these
world views divides by zero, or reads a zero as a real measurement. "Not computed yet" and
"genuinely zero" are the same two characters in the record, and a faction whose net income really
IS zero is a state the vocabulary is supposed to be able to represent — that is precisely what
na-s4e made representable.

This is the failure shape the project keeps meeting: a value that reports without having checked,
read as though it had checked. It is worse here than a missing field, because a missing field is
visibly missing and a zero looks like an answer.

SHAPE OF A FIX — decision needed, which is why this is a bead and not a patch:
  (a) omit the metrics block entirely when the aggregates are known stale, so the orchestrator
      sees a missing field rather than a false zero (directives already handle UNMEASURABLE, and
      _setback already omits rather than invents when the rate is absent);
  (b) emit the faction's aggregates only on surfaces where its turn IS being processed;
  (c) stamp the record with a freshness flag and let the orchestrator decide.

(a) is my recommendation — it uses the path that already exists for "cannot measure this", and it
makes the ambiguity unrepresentable rather than documented. Whoever owns the adapter's observation
path should pick.

title: metrics.energy_income reports gross base energy, not income — setback_turns is systematically optimistic
description:
metrics.energy_income reports GROSS base energy, not income: it omits facility maintenance and
commerce, so every setback_turns computed from it is systematically optimistic.

neural.cpp:404   na_buf_printf(w, ",\"energy_income\":%d", plr.energy_surplus_total);

energy_surplus_total is not net income:
  base.cpp:2307    per-base contribution is clamp(base->energy_surplus, 0, 99999) - a base in
                   energy deficit contributes 0, not a negative, so it is not even a true sum.
  game.cpp:1824-8  under RFLAG_INTEREST with rule_interest == 0, +1 per base is folded in here.
  game.cpp:1833    f->unk_17 = f->energy_surplus_total + f->turn_commerce_income
                               - f->facility_maint_total;
                   The engine computes true net SEPARATELY. So energy_surplus_total excludes
                   commerce and does not subtract maintenance.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE NAME. The value is the denominator of the only piece of hard
arithmetic the directive block shows a model:

  metrics.energy_income  ->  RATE_OF["energy_reserves"]  (directives.py:34)
                         ->  _setback: turns = abs(delta)/abs(rate)  (directives.py:430)
                         ->  setback_turns

A faction whose facility maintenance nearly consumes its gross energy is told that hurrying costs
a couple of turns of progress when the real recovery is far longer - or never, if net income is
<= 0, a case the current value cannot even represent because it is always >= 0.

_setback's docstring already names this failure mode: "A setback figure with an invented
denominator is worse than no figure, because it looks like the one piece of hard arithmetic in
the block." The denominator is not invented here, it is mislabelled, which is the same failure
with better paperwork. na_write_metrics' own docstring says "nothing here is estimated" - true of
the arithmetic, not of the name.

PROPOSED FIX - the engine's own expression, so it stays arithmetic rather than becoming an
estimate:

  na_buf_printf(w, ",\"energy_income\":%d",
      plr.energy_surplus_total + plr.turn_commerce_income - plr.facility_maint_total);

DECISION NEEDED, which is why this is a bead and not a patch: this changes the MEANING of a name
in the shared metrics vocabulary that directive evaluation divides by. The alternatives are (a)
change the value as above, (b) keep the value and rename the metric to something honest like
energy_gross, or (c) emit both. (a) is my recommendation - "income" is the name a directive
author will reach for, so the name should be right and the value should follow it. Whoever owns
metrics.py should pick.

NOT verified at runtime: no SMAC fixture on this host, so this is read from source across the
full chain rather than observed in a game. Found while working na-b4v, which asked for exactly
this metric's semantics to be checked rather than assumed.

title: Comms surfaces must issue directives - a diplomacy answer is a promise about later turns
description:
A diplomacy answer is a PROMISE about future turns, so the comms surface must issue a directive or the answer is a lie the game never notices.

Live case, turn 38 (2138), Peacekeepers vs Lord's Believers, status TREATY. Miriam:

  "Perhaps your troops failed to notice my large boundary markers when they illegally
   intruded into my territory. Would you kindly comply with our Treaty of Friendship by
   removing your forces at once?"

  1. "Withdraw troops to nearest base."
  2. "Only if you likewise withdraw from my territory!"
  3. "I have decided to make certain 'adjustments' to our borders, Miriam."

Option 1 commits us to move units OFF Believer tiles. Nothing in the current design carries that commitment past the dialog: the answer is applied to the diplomacy state and the conclusion dies with the response, which is the exact failure Directive was built for (contract.py, Directive docstring). The unit-movement decisions on later turns would have no idea a promise was made, so we would answer "yes, at once", leave the troops where they are, and take the treaty-break consequences without ever having decided to.

Option 2 is worse in the same way - it is a CONDITIONAL promise, so it also needs the condition tracked.

BLOCKED TWICE, both concrete:

1. METRIC VOCABULARY CANNOT EXPRESS IT (na-c17). Directive.metric must name something in
   metrics.py or the directive is rejected at issue time by design. The vocabulary is
   faction-level economics - energy_reserves, energy_income, labs_output, base_count, pop_total,
   military_units. There is no metric for "own units standing on another faction's territory",
   so the directive that this decision most obviously needs cannot be written at all. na-c17
   already says most directives cannot be expressed; this is a concrete, motivating instance of
   it rather than a new problem.

   The metric this case wants is roughly `units_in_foreign_territory` (count, lower is better,
   per-faction), which is also the metric that makes the promise CHECKABLE next turn - the whole
   point of the type. That is cheap for the adapter to compute: it already sweeps bases for
   drone_total, and a sweep over Vehs testing tile ownership is the same shape.

2. NOTHING WOULD RECEIVE IT. Even with the metric, directives reach a decision through
   relevant() - hop 0 matches an action whose `effects` touch the metric, or an entity the
   decision is about. There is no unit-movement LLM surface, and unit moves do not declare
   `effects`. So the directive would be in force, unmeasurable, and shown to nobody, which reads
   in the PlanBlock as a plan being served (unmeasurable, not unsatisfied) when it is inert.

ALSO BLOCKING THE SURFACE ITSELF: diplo.tribute is `demand_withdrawal` (engine.cpp:755), marked
in docs/game-surface.md as a raw engine pointer with no Thinker override - which is why it is one
of the ❌ rows. Intercepting it needs the central mod_popp wrapper (na-4lr). Until then the dialog
can only be driven through the na-input channel by clicking, which works but has no world view,
no action space and no decision record.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS FOR: the design rule, and the order of work. The rule is that any surface whose
answer is a commitment about later turns MUST issue a directive as part of its response, and the
acceptance for such a surface is not "it answered" but "a later turn acted on the answer".
diplo.tribute is the clearest instance because the promise is explicit and immediate, but
diplo.treaty_offer, diplo.surrender and the pact surfaces are all the same shape.

Suggested order: na-c17 (metric) -> a units/territory metric in the adapter -> na-4lr (dialog
interception) -> this surface. Doing the surface first produces a brain that makes promises
nothing can keep, which is worse than not having the surface.

Noted while trying to run this exact conversation through the brain: NA_BRAIN is "scripted" in
na.toml and there is no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment, so no real decision could be made
for it in that session either.

title: Multi-decision retrieval-ranking eval — one world view cannot measure a ranking rule
description:
na-373's refutation was withdrawn on re-measurement (see evals/runs/na-373/NOTES.md) and its
reversal is no more trustworthy. Both numbers reduce to a single fact's rank: 19 of 27 baseline
citations are fac:network-node, so 'citations in the top k' is really 'did network-node make the
cut'. The choice-stability half has the same defect from the other side — base.production at
turn 35 is 19/20 for one option, so an arm can only move it down, and a rule that keeps the
winner's fact looks harmless whatever else it does.

What would actually decide it:

- several world views, not one. Different surfaces (base.production, base.hurry, faction.tech)
  and different turns, so no single fact dominates the citation pool.
- contested decisions, chosen the way na-61c2 chooses its history arm — a near-unanimous world
  view cannot show a ranking doing damage OR doing good.
- score on aggregate citation rank across decisions (mean reciprocal rank or fraction-in-top-k
  pooled over all facts), not on one decision's choice flip.

Until that exists, ranking stays out of the retriever, and the reason recorded is 'unmeasured',
not 'refuted'.

    taken earlier records a value the engine then overwrites — and the record would disagree with

`just surfaces` computed "instrumented but switched off" from OBSERVED, so the new surface printed

such line: a surface can only be switched on if it has an apply path. That line read correctly

VERIFIED LIVE, and two findings about the remaining 26 that change how they should be picked.

## econ.energy_sliders confirmed from a running game

    faction: Gaians | turn 135
    native : econ 6 / labs 4 / psych 0  | energy_limit 10
    offered: 66 legal splits
    tier   : deterministic | applied: native

66 is the arithmetic checking out rather than my reading of it: all (labs, psych) with
labs+psych <= 10 is exactly 66, and energy_limit 10 excludes none of them. Three records in the
turn, one per routed faction. tier/applied confirm it observed without deciding.

## FINDING 1 — the ready bucket's volume filter is too narrow

`coverage()` computes volume_bound as `remaining - NO_AI_PATH` where `scope_for(s) == "unit"`. So
volume is treated as a property of UNIT scope.

base.specialists is base-scope and therefore counted "ready" — but `best_specialist()` is called
from a loop over `base->specialist_total` (base.cpp:2320-2325), for every specialist beyond the
16th, inside a block that itself runs several times per base-turn. On a 55-base faction that is
far higher volume than several unit-scope surfaces the partition excludes.

So "ready" currently means "has a native path and is not unit-scope", and it is being read as
"cheap to instrument". Those are different claims. A base-scope surface can be per-citizen.

Not fixing the partition here: changing what `ready` counts would move a number this project
quotes, and it deserves its own decision rather than being slipped in. Recorded so the next pick
is not made on a number that means something narrower than it looks.

## FINDING 2 — the seam IS most of the work; the 26 are not a batch

I tried to survey seams for ten of the remaining surfaces by grep and got nothing usable —
keyword hits across nine files each, because "where does the engine decide X" is not a textual
question. econ.energy_sliders took reading mod_allocate_energy end to end to learn that
SE_alloc_labs is narrowed four times and only the last value is real; that fact is what makes the
hook correct and no sweep would have surfaced it.

The two surfaces whose seams ARE now known:
    base.specialists   pick_specialist / best_specialist (base.cpp:4788) — high volume, see above
    econ.commerce      referenced in base.cpp, seam not yet read

Consequence for planning: each surface needs its decision function read before it can be ordered
by frequency and stakes at all, because frequency is a property of the CALL SITE and is not
visible from the registry. The pick order this bead asks for cannot be produced up front for all
26; it emerges one surface at a time.

## Pattern for the next one, established and verified

  1. find the engine function that settles the answer, and hook AFTER its last mutation
  2. build the action space from the engine's own constraint function, never from our reading
  3. land in OBSERVED, not APPLIED — the applied count is what says how much of the game the
     brain drives, and moving it for an observation overstates the one number kept honest
  4. run a game and confirm the record appears with a plausible action space

title: Evals: keep the committed runs honest as the prompt drifts
description:
evals/runs/ holds the prompts and answers behind every measured number in the docs, and evals/runs/<id>/manifest.json holds a sha256 of each prompt. Nothing checks it.

The failure is quiet and certain: the system prompt changes - it already has, twice - and the committed answers silently become evidence about a prompt that no longer exists, while just eval score keeps printing the same confident table. The docs then quote a number measured against something we no longer ship.

Cheapest fix is a test that regenerates each arm's prompt and compares the hash to the manifest, failing with 'the prompt moved, re-run the eval' rather than pretending. It needs THINKER_DIR to rebuild the world view, so it belongs behind the same skip the quipu tests use rather than in the default lane.

Better but more work: make the prompt reproducible without the sibling checkout by grounding from the committed datalinks/thinker/alphax.ttl instead of the fork's alphax.txt, which would let the check run everywhere.

Not urgent - both runs match their prompts today - but it is the difference between a stale eval announcing itself and a stale eval being believed.
close_reason:
just eval check compares each committed run's prompt hash against what the code produces now, and prints a unified diff of what moved. It found both evals stale immediately, in two different ways.

Ordinary drift: na-373 was measured, then _SYSTEM gained a history section for na-61c2. Re-ran both arms (40 Haiku decisions) so the committed run is current rather than once-true. The finding survived and strengthened - the ranking rule now predicts citation at 0.31 against 0.50 for chance, where the first measurement gave 0.43. Every number moved a little and none qualitatively.

The worse one: na-61c2's ARMS changed underneath it. It built its contested world view from ground(view, retriever, 4), which at the time meant the top four by information value, because the retriever briefly ranked before na-373 refuted it. Reverting that silently turned the same call into 'first four in action-space order' - a different fact set, a different experiment, the same name, and the old answers still sitting beside it scoring cleanly.

Fixed by naming the four facts in build_history.CONTESTED. The lesson is in evals/README.md: an eval's arms are part of the eval, and deriving them from whatever a component currently does means the experiment changes whenever that component does.

check deliberately does not judge whether drift matters - it says what moved and leaves that to a person, since some prompt changes cannot affect a given arm and asserting which is a claim needing its own evidence. Also fixed: the just eval recipe prefixed ../ unconditionally and broke on an absolute THINKER_DIR.

title: Retrieval cost on wide surfaces must be cut option-neutrally
description:
Follow-on from na-373, which refuted rank-then-truncate. Grounding is one fact per option, so any top-k truncation under-explains the options it drops and biases the choice - measured: truncating to the top 4 moved base.production from Network Node 19/20 to Research Hospital 15/20 and cut stability 0.95 to 0.75.

So the cost problem is still open and the shape of an acceptable fix is now known: it has to treat every option the same. Two candidates.

Uniform compression - shorten every fact rather than drop some. Cheapest to try, option-neutral by construction, and measurable with the existing harness.

Two-pass - a cheap fact for every option, rich facts only for a shortlist the brain asks about. Option-neutral in pass one. Costs a round trip on the highest-frequency surface, which is the thing to measure.

Measure with scripts/retrieval_utilisation.py: it already reports utilisation, mean cited, and the choice distribution, and the choice distribution is the half that matters. Acceptance is unchanged from na-373 - utilisation up with NO change to the choice distribution.

title: mdBook docs site
description: The repo had 18 design docs and no way to read them as a site. Set up mdBook with book.toml at the repo root pointing src at docs/ in place, rather than a docs/book/src/ copy: every doc already links its siblings by bare filename and is linked to from README.md and AGENTS.md as docs/<name>.md, so a book-specific source tree would have broken both the ~40 internal cross-references and every GitHub deep link, to render the same output.
close_reason: book.toml at the repo root, src = docs, build-dir = book (gitignored). docs/SUMMARY.md is the TOC across five sections and docs/README.md the index — it also gives the docs/ folder a landing page on GitHub. All 19 chapters render and every local link in the output resolves. Eight links escaping docs/ (six ../VISION.md, two into source files) became absolute GitHub URLs: mdBook rewrites .md to .html relative to the source root, so those resolved outside the book and 404'd. just docs gains build and serve; check is now lint plus build, because a chapter renamed without updating SUMMARY.md passes every markdown rule. CI's lint-markdown lane became docs and builds the book too — it also pinned markdownlint at 0.17.2, a third copy of the version that had drifted from the other two, now 0.23.2 everywhere. mdbook added to setup-environment.sh (release tarball, not cargo install — the lane budget is ~5 minutes) and the CONTRIBUTING tooling table.

title: Hank role (c)/(d): replace StateGuard with the real board graph
description:
StateGuard (orchestrator/hank.py) does the part of Hank role (c) that needs no board graph: it checks a chosen order's DECLARED effects against the metrics the world view reports. Denies what current state cannot pay for; warns on a violated directive.

That is a floor, not the design. What it cannot do without role (d):
  - reason about anything the adapter did not declare in Action.effects
  - check board-shaped preconditions (is the tile still ours, is the unit still alive, did the target base change hands)
  - what-if / speculative apply (role e)

TRACKED UPSTREAM (filed 2026-07-31):
  scbrown/hank#78  FR-35 generic non-code fact ingestion  <- the gate, everything depends on it
  scbrown/hank#79  FR-36 game-state policy selector model
  scbrown/hank#80  FR-37 hank_guard                       <- THIS issue blocks on #80
  scbrown/hank#81  FR-38 hank_whatif
  scbrown/hank#82  FR-39 per-game tenancy (a fog security boundary when >1 faction is LLM-driven)

Design doc: hank/docs/neuralamplifier-harness.md. Honest gating from that doc: all of FR-35..39 is net-new engineering, gated twice - by Hank Phase 4 (Phase 3 multi-tenancy has not started) AND by the non-code ingestion of FR-35, which does not exist. Every Hank node today anchors to a file:line span.

Also from that doc, and worth carrying into our expectations: hank_guard sees an APPROXIMATED post-order board, because applying orders to a COW overlay re-implements engine order semantics outside the engine. So deny stays conservative and the engine remains sole authority - which is the same precedence StateGuard already honours.

The seam is ready: StateGuard sits behind the Guard protocol, composed by GuardChain, so swapping in POST /guard should not change the verdict shape or the decision record.

title: Directive entity ids are cited as grounding facts and flagged as fabricated
description:
Hank's citation guard fires on 3-4 runs in 5 with 'cited facts that were never offered: fac:the-weather-paradigm'. The model is not hallucinating - it was genuinely shown that id, in a directive's entities list - but the guard reads the offered set only from the grounding block, so a directive entity looks fabricated.

Two id spaces that are deliberately the same (a directive's entities ARE grounding fact ids, which is what makes the multi-hop walk work) but only one of which counts as offered. The guard should treat ids shown in world_view.directives[].directive.entities as offered.

Left as a bug rather than fixed inline because it also inflates a real signal: utilisation counts cited-against-offered, and a citation the guard drops is currently invisible in both directions.
acceptance_criteria: A run where the only 'unoffered' citations are directive entities produces no advisory, and utilisation is unchanged by directives being present.
close_reason:
Already implemented on main; bead was left open. Verified rather than assumed.

Guard half: hank.py:81-82 builds the offered set as grounded_ids | entities_shown(world_view), and the code names na-zgz in its own comment. directives.py:304 entities_shown is the shared reader, deliberately NOT folded into grounding so the utilisation denominator does not move when a directive is present.

Utilisation half: knowledge.py summarise() splits citations into quipu_cited (retrieval, drives utilisation) and plan_cited (directive entities), so a legitimate citation is bucketed rather than dropped — which is what used to make it vanish from the record in both directions.

Acceptance covered by named tests, 12 passed: test_an_entity_a_directive_showed_is_offered_not_fabricated (no advisory) and test_a_genuinely_invented_id_is_still_caught_when_directives_are_present (a real hallucination is still flagged).

Second bead this session found shipped-but-open, after na-61c.2. bd ready is overstating remaining work.

title: Metric vocabulary is six faction fields deep; most directives cannot be expressed
description:
metrics.py holds 11 names and the adapter reports 6 faction-level ones. That covers economy and expansion, which is enough for the saving/expansion plans measured so far, but a directive about military posture, terraforming progress, tech position relative to rivals, or diplomatic standing cannot currently be written at all - the name does not exist, so it is refused at issue time.

The honest order of work is adapter first, vocabulary second: a name in the vocabulary that nothing reports produces directives that are permanently unmeasurable, which is the exact failure the closed vocabulary exists to prevent. drone_total is already in the vocabulary and NOT reported - it needs a sweep over bases - so it is the first thing to either emit or remove.

What is actually wanted: over a real run, per directive - attention rate (followed/in_force), override rate, and whether the metric moved toward its target. title: Decide the same world view N times to measure decision stability
description:
There is currently no way to tell a considered decision from a coin flip that happens to land on a legal option, because every measurement so far is a single sample.

Two Haiku runs on materially the same base.production world view produced different choices (Formers, then Colony Pod). The prompts were not identical, so that is suggestive rather than conclusive - which is exactly the problem: we cannot currently distinguish 'the model is unstable' from 'the prompts differed'.

Build a small harness that submits the SAME world view N times and reports the distribution of choices, plus the citation sets. Cheap, needs no game running (a captured world view from na-observations.jsonl is enough), and it gives three things nothing else does:
  - a stability number per surface, so 'this surface is decidable from what we send' becomes measurable
  - a regression check on world-view changes: if adding a field makes decisions MORE consistent, that is the field earning its place
  - a way to compare models on the same input without playing a game

Note the interaction with na-61c.2: if instability is real, recent-history context is the fix, and this harness is how you would know it worked.
acceptance_criteria: A script that takes a captured world view and a model, runs it N times, and reports choice distribution and mean utilisation; run against base.production and base.hurry with N>=5 and the results recorded in docs
notes:
FIRST MEASUREMENT TAKEN, controlled this time: five byte-identical prompts, Haiku, base.production at Gaia's Landing turn 35, 8 options, 7 facts offered.

  run 1  unit:0  Colony Pod   cited colony-pod, formers
  run 2  unit:0  Colony Pod   cited colony-pod
  run 3  unit:0  Colony Pod   cited colony-pod
  run 4  unit:1  FORMERS      cited formers, colony-pod
  run 5  unit:0  Colony Pod   cited colony-pod

  stability    0.80  (4 of 5 modal)
  utilisation  0.20 mean (1.4 of 7 facts cited)

So the instability recorded on na-61c.2 is REAL but modest - one flip in five on identical input, not the coin-flip the earlier uncontrolled pair suggested. That earlier observation (Formers vs Colony Pod) is now explained: it was most likely this same 1-in-5, not the prompt differences I hedged about.

Utilisation 0.20 with elimination-citations encouraged, against 0.14 when only the winning option's fact was asked for. Consistent with the na-373 finding that eliminations are real but few.

THE IMPORTANT RESULT is not the number. Run 5 stated 'nearly-complete Colony Pod (18/33 minerals done)'. The world view says minerals_accumulated = 4. It fabricated a state value it had been given correctly - and still reached the right decision, because it took the 15 turns from turns_if_continued rather than deriving it.

That is direct evidence for computing derived values in the adapter, and stronger than the argument that produced turns_if_switched/turns_if_continued in the first place. That change was made because the model got the ARITHMETIC wrong; this shows the precomputed field also insulates the decision when the model misreads the INPUTS. A world view that makes the brain derive things is a world view where a misread propagates into the choice.
close_reason: scripts/decision_stability.py does exactly what the AC asks: takes a captured world view plus a model, runs it N times, reports choice distribution and mean utilisation. Both named surfaces measured at N>=5 and recorded in docs: base.production N=5 (docs/decision-inputs.md:189-193, stability 0.80 / utilisation 0.20) and base.hurry N=10 (docs/directives.md:158-163, 0.60/1.00/0.80 across three plan configs). Extended since by claude_code_brain.py as a second measurement lane.

title: Measure whether LLM-tier decisions actually produce better outcomes
description:
On base.hurry the brain disagreed with the deterministic tier - it hurried a Colony Pod for 100 of 139 credits to save 15 turns, where Thinker declined. The justification was coherent and numerically grounded. Whether it was RIGHT is unknown, and nothing currently could tell us.

Every claim about decision quality so far is about legality, arithmetic and coherence - all of which are necessary and none of which is the actual goal. A brain that reasons beautifully into a worse position is the failure mode this project most needs to detect, and it is invisible in a single decision record.

What is needed is outcome measurement over a run: play the same save forward under llm_factions=0 and under the brain, and compare trajectories on the measures the game itself keeps - base count, mineral output, tech rate, military strength, faction score. The harness makes this feasible now: autoload is unattended, autosave runs every turn, and the world-view store keeps the bytes for replay.

Note the confound: any comparison must hold the fairness profile fixed, since an AI slot inherits difficulty handicaps a human slot does not (AGENTS.md invariant 6). Comparing an LLM-driven AI slot against a native AI slot at a different difficulty measures the handicap, not the brain.
acceptance_criteria: A repeatable A/B over at least 30 turns from an identical save, reporting the game's own score components for both arms, with the fairness profile recorded and identical across arms
notes:
BLOCKED IN PRACTICE by na-2mn (epic: expand the deterministic tier onto the 21 no-native-AI surfaces). bd will not record a task->epic dependency, so the link is recorded in notes on both issues.

The reason it blocks: an A/B needs a baseline. On the 21 NO_AI_PATH surfaces there is no native decision at all, so 'the brain decided X' cannot be scored against anything. Measurement on the four surfaces already instrumented (base.production, faction.tech, faction.se, base.hurry) can proceed now, because all four DO have a native answer - start there rather than waiting on the epic.

title: Narrow retrieval using the utilisation signal
description:
Grounding utilisation scales inversely with action-space width, measured with the same model, graph and retrieval path:

  base.production   8 options   7 facts offered   1 cited   utilisation 0.14
  base.hurry        2 options   1 fact offered    1 cited   utilisation 1.00

Retrieval currently fetches one fact per offered action, so a wide surface pays for facts the decision never turns on. Six of seven were unread on the production decision.

This is retrieval tuning, not prompting. Options, cheapest first:
1. Rank rather than fetch-all: keep the batched query, then order facts by relevance to the current state (e.g. affordable-this-turn first, category matching the base's evident need) and truncate. The token_budget machinery in datalinks/budget.py already truncates; it just has nothing to rank by.
2. Two-pass: cheap facts for every option, rich facts only for a shortlist the brain asks about. Costs a round trip.
3. Learn from citations: fact ids are stable across turns and runs by construction, so accumulated citation counts per (surface, fact) are a usable prior. This is the K3 learned-memory path and depends on na-bdn.

Start with 1. Measure utilisation before and after over the same set of decisions - the instrumentation makes this a number rather than an argument.
acceptance_criteria: Utilisation on base.production rises materially over a sample of at least 20 decisions with no drop in decision quality; the ranking rule is documented and its inputs come from the world view rather than from the graph alone
notes:
PREMISE TESTED AND REFINED - the original framing over-claimed, but the conclusion survives.

The worry was that utilisation 0.14 measured citation CONVENTION rather than waste: a brain that compares 8 options and cites the 1 that won has arguably used all 7 facts, 6 of them to eliminate. So the same decision was re-run asking for citations in three buckets - facts that supported the choice, facts that helped RULE OUT an option, and facts that influenced nothing.

Result:
  DECIDED     unit:colony-pod                         1
  ELIMINATED  fac:recreation-commons                  1
  UNUSED      5 facts, named explicitly by the model  5

So eliminations are real but rare - one, not six - and utilisation rises only from 0.14 to 0.29. Five of seven facts influenced nothing by the model's own account. The waste is real and worth reducing.

Two caveats to carry forward, both of which weaken the number without overturning it:
  - Self-reported 'unused' is weak evidence. A model's introspection about what influenced it is not reliable, and this is the best signal available rather than a good one.
  - Utilisation should COUNT eliminations. Measuring only what supported the winner systematically under-reports, so the instrumentation's definition of 'cited' must include 'helped rule out'. That is a semantics change in what we ask the brain for, not a schema change - Orders.cited already carries a list.

Revised approach: keep ranking as the fix, but do NOT rank by desirability. Ranking cheap-and-soon options first would ground the affordable options better than the expensive ones, which biases the choice through retrieval - a worse failure than wasted tokens, and an invisible one. Rank by expected information value instead: an option whose name does not imply its effect needs a fact; 'Scout Patrol' largely does not.

title: Central mod_popp wrapper: intercept in-game dialogs as decision points
description:
Wrap the engine's dialog function popp(filename, label, a3, pcx_filename, fn) (engine.h:667) so every in-game dialog is visible to the adapter and routable to Claude.

This is invariant 7 made real: 'Intercept in-game dialogs; never blanket-suppress them. They are decision points.' Council votes, diplomacy offers, random events and pact proposals all arrive as popp dialogs, and each is a decision surface the brain should own. Only Thinker's fatal-error MessageBoxA should ever be suppressed.

Precedent exists: Thinker already hooks individual popp call sites - base_production_popp at patch.cpp:681 and BaseWin_staple_popp at 753-754 - so wrapping centrally is the same technique applied once instead of per site. Identify dialogs by (filename, label), which is what the call already passes.

IMPORTANT distinction, do not conflate these:
  - IN-GAME dialogs (events, diplomacy, council) are decisions. Intercept, emit a surface_id, route to the LLM tier where appropriate. Core architecture, and a whole class of surfaces at once.
  - MENU and file-picker chrome (the LOAD dialog) is not a decision, just startup plumbing. Do NOT build automation for it - fix the -na-autoload menu-to-session transition instead so no picker is ever needed. Automating the picker is throwaway work.

Note also that the LOAD picker is not a popp dialog and runs its own message pump, which is why the command channel goes deaf inside it (see na-abc).
acceptance_criteria: A single hook observes every popp dialog with its filename and label; each observed dialog is recorded with a surface_id; a documented allowlist controls which are auto-answered vs routed vs passed through to the human; Thinker's fatal-error MessageBoxA remains suppressed and nothing else is blanket-suppressed

title: Command channel goes deaf inside the engine's modal dialogs
description:
The in-DLL command channel (thinker fork, na_command_tick) is polled from ModWinProc. The engine's modal dialogs - the LOAD file picker among them - run their own message pump, so the window procedure stops being called and the channel stops responding while one is open. Verified: a 'shot' and a 'click' issued with the LOAD dialog open produced no result file at all.

The dialog is drawn INSIDE the game window rather than as a native Windows control (xdotool sees no separate X window for it), so it is not separately addressable from outside either. External input does not reach this game in any case - it reads the mouse through DirectInput under a Wine virtual desktop.

Consequence: automation can open a modal dialog but cannot act inside one. That is enough to reach the LOAD picker and no further, which is exactly one click short of useful.

Candidate fixes:
1. Hook something that runs during modal pumps. popp() and the Console/dialog handlers are the obvious candidates - find one that is unconditionally patched.
2. Avoid dialogs entirely: fix the -na-autoload menu-to-session transition so no picker is ever needed. That is the better goal and is tracked separately as the load_game transition bug.
3. A timer-based tick (SetTimer plus a WM_TIMER handler, or a worker thread) that survives modal pumps. A thread would need care - the engine is not thread-safe.

Approach 2 makes this issue moot for the resume use case, which is the only current consumer. Prefer it.
notes:
Confirmed WORSE than originally described, and now moot for the resume use case.

A worker thread does NOT survive modal dialogs. Input was moved onto a dedicated thread on the reasoning that PostMessage is thread-safe and a thread is independent of the message pump. A heartbeat counter disproved it: the thread ticked normally at the startup screen, froze at the exact instant the picker opened, and never resumed while the process stayed alive. Two plausible causes were tested and eliminated - the picker does not change the working directory, and switching the thread from stdio to Win32 file APIs did not help despite Thinker sharing a single global FileLock with the game (patch.cpp:14-20).

So the constraint is architectural: while a modal dialog is open, NO code of ours runs. Anything needing interaction inside a modal is unreachable.

Moot for resume because na-c9f is solved by never opening a modal (QUICK START instead of LOAD GAME). Keep this open only as a documented limit - if some future surface genuinely needs input inside a modal, the answer is probably to avoid that dialog, not to defeat the pump.

Separate finding worth its own note: in-game input does not reach the engine through posted messages at all. The startup screen and dialogs accept WM_LBUTTONDOWN / WM_KEYDOWN; the map UI does not - it reads DirectInput. So ending a turn cannot be driven from outside the process, which is why an 'observe <base_id>' test hook exists in the DLL.
close_reason:
Closing as a documented limitation, not a fix. There is no code left to write and it has been cluttering the ready pool.

The bead's own notes record it is WORSE than filed and moot for the motivating case: a dedicated worker thread does NOT survive a modal dialog (heartbeat froze at the instant the picker opened and never resumed), and the two plausible causes were tested and eliminated. So the candidate fixes are dead ends, not unattempted work.

The mitigation shipped: -na-autoload reaches a playable session via click_quickstart / confirm_planetfall (thinker src/neural.cpp:2250,2264) rather than the LOAD picker, so automation never needs to act inside the modal that motivated this.

The limit is documented at docs/thinker-adapter-notes.md:202. Re-observed this session while driving turns: the command channel goes silent during a modal and returns when it closes, exactly as described - so the documentation is accurate and current.

title: bd export with no -o writes to stdout, silently leaving the tracked JSONL stale (docs/UX)
description:
`bd export` with NO output path can write a STALE JSONL — silently, and in the one direction
that loses work. Measured 2026-08-03 while closing na-1p2.

## Reproduction, exact

    bd -C <na> close na-1p2 ...
    bd -C <na> show na-1p2 --json   -> status: closed, closed_at: 2026-08-03T07:43:43Z   (live store, correct)
    bd dolt commit                  -> "Nothing to commit."                              (working set clean)

    cd <na> && bd export                       # default path .beads/issues.jsonl
      issues.jsonl says: in_progress | closed_at: None      <-- STALE

    bd export -o /tmp/na-fresh.jsonl           # explicit path, same store, seconds later
      fresh export says: closed | closed_at: 2026-08-03T07:43:43Z   <-- CORRECT

Same binary, same store, same second. The ONLY difference is whether an output path was given.

## Why this is the mechanism behind two prior incidents

`.beads/export-state.json` carries `{"last_dolt_commit": ..., "timestamp": ..., "issues": 69}`.
The default-path export is watermark-gated on it; the explicit-path export is a full live dump.
When the watermark says nothing changed, the default export rewrites the file from the stale
snapshot rather than declining to write — so it produces a COMPLETE-LOOKING file with the right
id count and the wrong field values.

That is exactly the signature recorded on this repo before:
  - 36d67d0 "export the embedded store to JSONL — 14 beads existed only in local Dolt"
  - 3a0158a "restore nine closes that the last export reverted"
Both were repaired by hand. Neither identified why, and the id-set check that came out of them
CANNOT catch this: the id set is identical (69 before, 69 after, none added, none removed). Only
a per-record FIELD diff catches it, which is why that rule exists — and this is the first time
the rule has actually fired rather than being a precaution.

## Workaround (use this until fixed)

    bd export -o /tmp/fresh.jsonl && cp /tmp/fresh.jsonl .beads/issues.jsonl

then diff BOTH the id set AND the field values against a pre-write snapshot before committing.
Script used here: it fails the run if any id disappeared, if any record went closed -> not-closed,
if a record this write did not touch moved at all, or if the intended change is ABSENT (which is
the case that fired today).

## Severity

A stale export is not a cosmetic issue on this repo: the JSONL is the git-tracked tracker, so a
stale write silently REVERTS closed beads for everyone who pulls, and the revert looks like a
normal export commit. It has already cost two manual repairs.

NOT YET INVESTIGATED: whether the watermark is stale because `bd close` does not advance it, or
because the embedded engine commits without updating export-state. Both are cheap to check.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
## RETRACTION — my headline claim was FALSE, and sattler was right to push on it

I filed this as "`bd export` with no -o writes a STALE JSONL — the mechanism behind the two
close-reverting incidents". **Both halves of that are wrong.** Correcting it in full rather than
quietly editing, because a confident wrong bug report sends the next person to the wrong layer.

### What is actually true (measured twice, on two different stores)

`bd export` with no `-o` writes to **STDOUT**. It does not touch `.beads/issues.jsonl` at all.

    bd export --help:  "-o, --output string   Output file path (default: stdout)"

    NA store, same file, side by side:
      mtime BEFORE  2026-08-03 03:52:34.593697731   md5 714332b78156
      $ bd export >/dev/null            # no -o
      mtime AFTER   2026-08-03 03:52:34.593697731   md5 714332b78156   <- IDENTICAL

    Clean throwaway store (bd init --prefix zz): default export printed one JSON line to stdout
    and `.beads/issues.jsonl` was never created at all.

So there is no "stale export code path". What happened to me was simpler and entirely my own
error: I ran `bd export`, discarded stdout, then read the pre-existing `.beads/issues.jsonl` and
reported its OLD contents as "the export". `bd export -o <path>` looked like a different, correct
code path only because it is the one that wrote a file at all.

My verify script was right — "the intended change is NOT in the export" — and I misread WHY. It
was not a bad export; it was no export.

### The two prior incidents are NOT this, and their own commit messages say so

sattler's point stands and the evidence is in the history:

  36d67d0 — 14 beads "absent from the live store entirely ... no delete or tombstone event".
            Records missing from the STORE. A correct export faithfully wrote out a store that
            was already wrong. Its repair used the EXPLICIT `-o` form, i.e. my "correct" arm.
  3a0158a — "the export took the store as authoritative and wrote it over a JSONL that was more
            correct than the store", and every affected record "had a store record whose
            updated_at PREDATED its own close_at". Lost writes IN THE STORE.

Both are store-side (the aegis-t15jl family: embedded-store writes not sticking). Mine was a
reading error. **They are not the same defect and I should not have joined them.** I reached for
one mechanism to explain two prior incidents plus my own observation, which is how a tidy story
beats a true one.

### What IS still a real footgun, downgraded to what it is

`bd export` with no `-o` succeeds, prints to stdout, exits 0, and leaves the git-tracked JSONL
untouched. A workflow that runs `bd export` expecting the tracked file to update gets a stale
tracked file and no signal — which is exactly what bit me. That is a UX/docs sharp edge worth a
line in the bd docs or a warning when stdout is not a TTY and a tracked `.beads/issues.jsonl`
exists. It is NOT data corruption and NOT P1.

Re-prioritising this bead to P3 and rewriting the title accordingly.

### One thing I observed and have NOT explained — flagged as UNTESTED, not asserted

At the moment of my close, `.beads/issues.jsonl` (03:43:42.538) and `.beads/export-state.json`
(03:43:42.544) were written 6 ms apart, which looks like one export operation. A later probe
(`bd comment`) did NOT move either file, and config.yaml mentions an auto-backup `interval: 15m`,
so an interval-gated auto-export is a plausible explanation for both the write and for it
carrying pre-close state.

**Plausible is not measured.** I am recording it as an open question rather than a second
mechanism, having just been burned for exactly that move. If an interval-gated auto-export does
capture pre-write state, that WOULD be a genuine stale-write path and belongs upstream — but
someone has to prove it first.

### Upstream

sattler is right that if this reproduces against any store it belongs upstream with this bead as
evidence. The reproducible part does: default-export-to-stdout is bd behaviour, not na behaviour,
and it reproduced on a clean `bd init` store. The na-specific parts (the two prior incidents) do
not — they are store-side and already tracked as aegis-t15jl.

title: just docs check is red repo-wide on MD060 table-column-style
description:
Nineteen files — every doc with a table, plus AGENTS.md, README.md and VISION.md — fail 'just docs check' with MD060 'Table pipe is missing space' for the compact style. The pre-push gate 'just check' passes, because its markdownlint hook and the docs recipe do not run the same rule set; only the docs recipe enforces MD060.

That split is the actual problem. AGENTS.md tells you to run 'just check' before pushing and 'just docs build' if docs changed, so a doc change lands green while 'just docs check' has been red for long enough that nobody can tell which failures are new. A gate that is always red is not a gate.

Two ways out and they need a decision, not a sweep: reformat every table to the compact style and keep MD060, or disable MD060 in .markdownlint-cli2.yaml and stop claiming to enforce it. Whichever, the two configs should agree afterwards.

(2) All 388 MD060 violations fixed with --fix across 19 files: table separator rows go |---|---| to | --- | --- |, plus one double-space in an empty header cell. Rendering is unchanged. Both `just check` and `just docs check` are green.
